• Figure 1c includes subjects over the age of 20, can you explain their inclusion?”
Participants up to age 25 were included in order to capture the full developmental trajectory
relevant to epilepsy in pediatric and young adult populations. White matter microstructure and
thalamocortical pathways continue to mature through the mid-twenties. Including young adults
allowed us to better represent the continuum of structural variation and seizure outcomes. The
age range is now explicitly reported under Clinical data do not predict response after VNS.
“We compiled the largest database of children to undergo VNS (n = 1046) from 11 North
American centers through the Connectomics and Vagus Nerve Stimulation Outcome Study
(CONNECTiVOS, Fig. 1a).28 Participants were deemed responders if seizure frequency was
reduced by ≥80% and non-responders if ≤20% (n = 694, Fig. 1b) to reflect the bimodal
distribution of seizure outcomes and mitigate the effects of ambiguous intermediate outcomes.29
The mean [SD; range] age was 10.6 [4.7; 0.8-24.2] years, 54% male and included 51%
responders (Fig. 1b-c). Participants up to age 25 were included to capture the full
developmental trajectory of brain maturation amongst pediatric and young adult populations
that undergo VNS.”
The manuscript could benefit from a deeper/more explicit discussion of the heterogenous age
distribution of subjects and how this variation could affect indications of atrophy and findings
related to serotonin networks.
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Given that our study involves a pediatric
population with substantial developmental variability, we carefully accounted for age in every
aspect of our analyses. For this reason, the VQ-VAE representation learning model was trained
on a dataset of T1w MRI images across the lifespan, ranging from 1 to 89 years old. In
Supplementary Figure 8, we demonstrate that variability in cortical thickness across the cohort
was primarily driven by age, rather than site or outcome, with a significant age-related
component (r = -0.45, p = 6.7e-14). This confirms that age is a major contributor to variability in
cortical thickness data, but these features are not predictive of response to VNS.
To directly assess potential effects of age-related cortical changes on VNS outcomes, we
examined the relationship between regional cortical thickness and treatment response.
FreeSurfer-derived cortical thickness measures were entered into general linear models
predicting VNS response, with age and intracranial volume included as covariates
(Supplementary Table 3). To assess stability across age, we re-ran these analyses after
dichotomizing the cohort by median age (Table R1 shown below). Across both the full and age-
split samples, cortical thickness was not associated with VNS response in any region of the
brain, indicating that age-related variability does not explain group differences.
In addition, our cortical atrophy analysis explicitly accounted for age, as atrophy maps were
computed relative to age- and sex-matched healthy controls within the lesion network mapping
framework. This design ensures that apparent cortical thinning reflects pathological deviation
from expected developmental trajectories rather than normative developmental effects.
We have now included a more explicit discussion on how age could affect indications of atrophy
and the implication it has on our findings.
“The VQ-VNS model demonstrated predictive accuracy across the pediatric age span. In the
CONNECTiVOS cohort, we demonstrate that a child’s chronological age at implantation is
not associated with VNS outcomes. Rather, a pattern of brain atrophy characterized by the
VQ-VNS salience map predicts response across development (Supplementary Fig. 7c). 
Convergence of the salience map with the LNM analysis – wherein brain atrophy is
parametrized relative to normative age- and sex-matched developmental trajectories – supports
a framework where structural brain changes drive VNS response.”

• Please revise the claims on lines 206-208. The model’s poor performance on out-of-distribution
data generally does not suggest any specificity to VNS, especially given that the model was pre
trained on healthy non-VNS patients. This likely reflects domain shift or lack of
representativeness in training data, and less likely biological specificity.
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. To clarify, while the encoder-decoder was
pretrained on healthy subjects, the support vector machine (SVM) classifier itself was trained
exclusively on the VNS cohort. As such, the features driving classification were deviations from
healthy anatomy that were specifically associated with VNS outcomes. The poor generalization
to the temporal lobectomy (TLE) cohort therefore suggests that the latent features of T1w images
that predict VNS response do not directly translate to prediction of post-surgical seizure
outcomes. We have revised the text to avoid implying biological specificity to VNS, instead
emphasizing that the learned decision boundary is informative for VNS outcomes but not for
resection outcomes. This has been made clearer in the text:
“To evaluate the specificity of the SVM to predicting VNS outcomes, we tested its
performance on an independent cohort of children who underwent temporal lobectomy for
temporal lobe epilepsy39 (n = 102; mean age [SD] = 12.8 [3.9] years; 69.6% seizure freedom).
The SVM model did not generalize to this cohort (AUC = 0.57, p = 0.12; Fig. 3g), suggesting
that its decision boundary is not applicable to this population.”

• Explain the choice and dimensionality of the 32-dimension feature space on line 196.”
The 32-dimensional feature space corresponds to the latent embeddings produced by the VQ-
VAE model, which were then aggregated across space for each subject. This dimensionality was
chosen based on the VQ-VAE implementation in Tudosiu et. al, 2024, where this latent size was
shown to balance reconstruction fidelity and representational compactness. In our case, the 32-
dimensional representation provided strong reconstruction accuracy and yielded stable features
for downstream classification, so we retained this configuration. We have revised the Methods to
clarify the chosen dimensionality of the feature space by citing the original work it was based on
as well as what the dimensions represent. In addition, we have included the dimensions in Figure
2.

• Explain the choice of using an SVM as the classifier for the embeddings rather than an
ensemble of models or other alternatives (random forest etc.). I strongly suggest comparing
different modeling strategies, where applicable.
Our choice of SVM as the classifier for the learned embeddings was guided by both theoretical
considerations and empirical evaluation. Among several standard classifiers tested, including
logistic regression, random forest, and k-nearest neighbors (kNN), SVM consistently provided
the best balance between model complexity, robustness to overfitting, and predictive accuracy on
held-out data. Logistic regression tended to underfit, random forests showed overfitting
tendencies, and kNN performed less favorably overall.
These comparisons are now presented in Supplementary Figure 6, which confirms that the SVM
achieved the highest classification accuracy for the learned latent representations. Together,
these results support its selection as the final classifier in the VQ-VNS framework.

• In evaluating the cortical thickness estimation, explain the choice behind using t-SNE vs other
techniques. What are its benefits and shortcomings?
We used t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) as a dimensionality reduction
technique to visualize cortical thickness patterns in a two-dimensional space24 . t-SNE is widely
used for examining high-dimensional data because it preserves local structure and highlights
neighbourhood relationships between subjects. This makes it ideal for visualizing subtle
grouping patterns in complex neuroimaging datasets. We recognize, however, that t-SNE also
has important limitations. The resulting embeddings can be sensitive to hyperparameters and
initializations, and global distances are not well preserved, which may complicate interpretation.
Nonetheless, for our goal of exploring relative clustering and qualitative separation of cortical
thickness patterns across subjects, t-SNE provides an effective and widely accepted
dimensionality-reduction tool that enabled effective visualization and quantitative analysis. We
have included a brief discussion in the revised manuscript.
“To evaluate potential site-related batch effects in the cortical thickness data, we applied t-
distributed stochastic neighbor embedding24 (t-SNE) to all cortical vertex values and estimated
total intracranial volumes (eTIV), projecting them into two dimensions. To preserve local
neighbourhood structure in high-dimensional data, t-SNE was selected. Although t-SNE does
not preserve global distances well, it offers an established and effective visualization tool for
our goal of exploring relative clustering and assessing potential batch effects. Embeddings
were visualized by site (Supplementary Fig. 9a), outcome, and age (Supplementary Fig. 9b–c).
Age showed the strongest correlation with t-SNE component 1 (Supplementary Fig. 9d). As no
consistent clustering by site was observed, no further harmonization was applied.”
• Explain the choice between permuting model outcomes versus other model comparison
techniques.
The use of permutation testing was not intended as an alternative, but rather as a complementary
evaluation to provide an empirical significant estimate of the observed AUC. The purpose of the
permutation analysis is to demonstrate that the model performs significantly better than chance,
which reflects the baseline level of current clinical decision-making. By permuting the labels,
we demonstrate that mismatched labels yield a null distribution of performance, confirming that the
observed accuracy arises from the model learning a mapping between T1 features and outcome
rather than chance. We have added clarification in the text.
In the revised manuscript, we now also report a full suite of conventional metrics (accuracy,
precision, recall, F1, and specificity) in addition to permutation testing (permuting the test/train
split with refitting and retesting). Our goal is to provide a comprehensive assessment of model
performance, using both conventional measures and permutation-based evaluation for
robustness.
“Robustness was assessed by permutation testing with 1,000 label shuffles to generate a null
distribution of AUC scores, enabling empirical significance estimation. This procedure tests
whether the VQ-VNS model’s observed performance exceeds chance expectations, thereby
confirming that predictions reflect a learned mapping between input features and outcome.”
• In order to improve potential clinical applicability, consider framing predictions as probability
scores of response (e.g. P(Response|Input)) rather than binary outputs.
We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. We agree that probabilistic predictions
would improve clinical applicability. In our current implementation using a linear SVM,
however, the decision boundary is very fine, resulting in most samples lying close to the
separating hyperplane. While this behavior is appropriate for the model’s internal decision-
making, the distance from the decision boundary in our implementation does not yield
confidence scores with a wide enough range to support clinical decision making, given the fine-
grained separation in this dataset.
In our revised manuscript, we have presented results for a probabilistic Logistic Regression
model (Supplementary Figure 7), but future work exploring probabilistic classifiers or
approaches explicitly designed to calibrate output probabilities will be required to generate
probability scores that are better suited to support clinician decision making. We have added this
as a future direction in the Discussion.
“Finally, future work should incorporate probabilistic classifiers to yield confidence
estimates that better support clinician decision-making.”

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Clinical
Researchers developed VQ-VNS, a deep learning model that predicts the effectiveness of vagus
nerve stimulation (VNS) for children with epilepsy using routine preoperative MRI scans.
Traditional clinical data could not predict treatment response, but VQ-VNS achieved significant
predictive accuracy and highlighted serotonin-rich brain regions and connectivity disruptions in
non-responders. These results are clinically relevant and highly translational, offering a
biologically interpretable tool to guide decisions and reduce unnecessary invasive procedures.
Methods
Patient grouping: Participants were divided into >80% seizure reduction vs. <20%. What about
patients between these cut-offs? Excluding ~350 patients (694/1046 included) seems a large data
loss. Since you collected seizure frequency reduction as a continuous variable, would correlating
with this continuous measure be more informative?
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We are keenly aware that patient and
parent-reported seizure frequency reductions are less reliable in intermediate ranges, introducing
uncertainty and potential misclassification in outcome labeling.20 To minimize this bias – and to
represent the bimodal distribution of the data – we restricted the primary analysis to participants
at the extremes of response (>80% or <20% seizure reduction), where outcome classification is
most reliable. While this approach necessarily reduced the sample size, it ensured greater label
validity and outcome confidence for model training and evaluation.
To assess the robustness of this decision, we conducted a secondary analysis including
participants with intermediate seizure reductions (20-80%). Even under this broader inclusion
criterion, the model maintained above-chance (albeit reduced) prediction accuracy, supporting
the generalizability of the learned representations despite increased label uncertainty.
Clinical outcomes: In the analysis section, you note that including patients with ambiguous
outcomes did not improve SVM performance. This is an important observation — why not
include them in the main analysis if results are unchanged? Please clarify the added value of
excluding them.
As noted, including participants with intermediate or ambiguous outcomes did not substantially
change overall SVM performance. However, we opted to retain the stricter outcome definition in
the primary analysis to ensure that the model was trained on the most reliable and biologically
meaningful labels. Incorporating uncertain outcomes can artificially stabilize accuracy metrics
by introducing label noise that the model effectively “averages out,” but this does not guarantee
that the learned representations are clinically valid.
By training on well-defined extremes (>80% and <20% seizure reduction), we ensured that the
learned embeddings reflect robust neurobiological differences between clear responders and non-
responders. The secondary analysis including intermediate cases serves as a complementary
robustness check, confirming that model performance remains stable even when label
uncertainty is increased.
Clinical variables: Have magnet effects and quality of life (QOL) been addressed? Both are well-
established as clinically relevant (Danthine V., Boon P.), and could enrich the dataset. If
available, these should be included.
We completely agree that these are very important considerations. Unfortunately, these data were
not available for the majority of subjects in our cohort. Our study was not sufficiently powered to
evaluate QoL outcomes in relation to imaging-derived predictors. Moreover, part of the novelty
of the present work lies in demonstrating that treatment response can be predicted using only a
structural T1-weighted MRI, without requiring additional clinical variables. We agree that
integrating magnet effects and QoL would enrich future models when larger, multimodal
datasets become available.
SVM classifier: Only 263 patients were included after excluding those with prior surgery or
significant abnormalities. Please describe their clinical characteristics. Were they representative
of the larger cohort (e.g., intellectual disability, DEEs, epilepsy duration)? The generalizability
of the model is limited if large patient groups are excluded.
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. As expected, this exclusion led to a
marginally lower proportion of patients with developmental delay, which frequently occurs with
structural abnormalities. Conversely, a greater proportion of generalized-onset epilepsies were
observed in the analyzed subset, consistent with the exclusion of focal lesional cases. A smaller
proportion of the 263 patients included in model training had a development delay and
generalized onset seizures. These differences represent a limitation of our training set, which did
not include abnormal brains. Overall, the included patients remained demographically and
clinically representative of the broader VNS cohort with respect to age, response, and other
underlying etiology. These characteristics are now summarized in Supplementary Table 12
alongside those of the excluded patients.
We note in the Discussion that, because patients with abnormal brain anatomy were excluded
(approximately 10% of the screened cohort), model generalizability to these cases has yet to be
determined.
“Third, images with significant anomalies or motion artifact were excluded from response
prediction because the pretraining datasets did not include images with significant anatomical
abnormalities. This may limit generalizability to grossly abnormal brains, which represented
<10% of our datasets (45 out of 489 images screened, Supplementary Fig. 4).”

Thank you for the opportunity to clarify. The CONNECTIVOS registry is a prospective study

were not systematically enrolled. For the purpose of evaluating model specificity, we utilized an
independent, previously published, retrospective cohort of patients19 who underwent temporal
lobectomy because high-quality preoperative imaging and clinical outcome data were available
for this group.
Not all patients in the TLE cohort achieved seizure freedom (~60%), allowing us to evaluate
model behavior across a clinically heterogeneous but well-characterized surgical population. We
focused on TLE because it represents the most common and well-defined surgical epilepsy
subgroup, enabling a more controlled assessment of whether the learned VNS-related imaging
representations generalize to a distinct treatment population.
“To evaluate the specificity of the VQ-VNS model’s performance, we tested its ability to predict
seizure freedom in a separate cohort of patients with temporal lobe epilepsy26–28 (TLE) who
underwent temporal lobectomy (n = 102; mean age [SD] = 12.8 [3.9] years; 69.6% seizure
freedom). This retrospective TLE cohort was selected because high-quality preoperative T1-
weighted imaging and detailed postoperative outcome data were available, enabling an
assessment of whether the VQ-VNS model, training exclusively on VNS recipients, generalizes
to an independent surgical population. In this cohort, approximately 70% of patients achieved
seizure freedom following surgery, which enabled the evaluation of model specificity. T1-
weighted images were acquired using Philips and GE scanners (Achieva, Genesis Signa, Signa
HDxt, Signa Excite) with field strengths of 1.5T or 3T. Imaging parameters were: flip angle =
13.6° (range: 8.0°–30.0°), echo time = 4.3 ms (2.3–4.6 ms), repetition time = 8.7 ms (5.0–25.0
ms), and mean voxel size = 0.9 × 0.9 × 1.4 mm. Abnormal images were excluded in this cohort
similar to the VNS cohort.”
Methodological consistency: For the VNS analysis, patients with brain lesions were excluded. Is
this a methodological requirement, and if so, why would it not apply to the surgical cohort?
We thank the reviewer for noting this inconsistency. We excluded patients with brain lesions
from the VNS analysis because there was insufficient representation of specific lesion types to
allow the model to learn meaningful representations of these more heterogenous and
anatomically variable abnormalities. As such, it performs optimally on brains that are
morphologically closer to normative anatomy.
To ensure methodological consistency, we have now applied the same exclusion criteria to the
surgical cohort to ensure methodological consistency across analyses. After this additional
quality control step, the surgical test set comprised 102 subjects. The updated model for TLE did
not improve above chance, supporting specificity to VNS (ROC-AUC of 0.57, p = 0.12).

Would comparison to a DBS cohort (ANT, CM) be more appropriate than only TLE?
We completely agree that comparison to patients with DBS would provide valuable context. We
also have a prospective registry of DBS in children, however, at present, our dataset does not
include a sufficient number of DBS cases to permit a meaningful inclusion.
Definitions: How was developmental delay defined, and does this overlap with DEE cases?
Developmental delay was reported by each participating site according to their local clinical
assessment, independent of whether or not the participant met criteria for a developmental
epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). As such, the designation may reflect a heterogeneous set of
clinical criteria, and we acknowledge this as a limitation.
As the reviewer suggests, there is likely an overlap between cases labeled as “developmental
delay” and patients who might also meet criteria for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
(n = 180).
Parameters: The discussion states VNS was “optimally programmed.” Please define this — were
parameters such as rapid cycling or saturation cycling considered (e.g., Norpulse study)?
We thank the reviewer for this important point. In our study, VNS programming
parameters were not standardized. They were left to the discretion of the treating clinicians at
individual sites. This variability is a limitation of the study and is discussed in the revised
manuscript. We did request stimulation parameter data, though they were only available for
n=103. Within this cohort, the average output current was 1.8mA and the average duty cycle was
20%. There was no difference in output current (1.90.7 vs. 1.70.7; t=-1.4; p=0.17; n=103) or
duty cycle (2110% vs. 1910%; t=-1.3, p=0.2, n=103) between responders and non-responders.
No patient received rapid cycling or saturation cycling.
“This study has several limitations. First, while VNS implantation is highly standardized with
minimal inter-subject variability, stimulation parameters were not standardized across sites and
were adjusted at the discretion of the treating clinician, leading to potential differences in the
charge density delivered. However, among participants with available data (N=103), mean
stimulation parameters (output current 1.8mA; duty cycle 20%) were consistent with optimally
programmed populations.26”
Data splitting: The dataset was split 80/10/10 for training/validation/test. What is the rationale
for this choice? Did results vary with different splits (e.g., 50/25/25)? Please provide references
or justification.
Yes, changing the split would change model performance. The dataset was divided into training,
validation, and test sets using a stratified split that approximated an 75/10/15 distribution, to
provide greater power for out-of-sample evaluation on the test set. This strategy maximized the
size of the training set while retaining sufficient subjects for validation and robust assessment on
a held-out test cohort, which is commonly used in the context of clinical datasets. 27–29 While
other splits are possible, an 80% training allocation is standard practice for clinical machine
learning applications.
To confirm that our results were not dependent on a single random partition, we repeated model
training across multiple randomized splits through repeated-holdout cross validation. The
resulting distribution from 1000 splits demonstrated that that latent features predict VNS
response at AUCs significantly above chance (p < 0.001; mean = 0.613). Importantly, our
original withheld dataset did not represent an outlier within this randomly permuted distribution
(p ≈ 0.2, based on 1,000 random splits). These results support the stability of our model’s ability
to predict VNS outcomes beyond what would be expected by chance alone.
“To balance retaining a sufficient training set size with sufficient subjects for validation and
robust assessment on a held-out test cohort, these data were split into training, validation and
test sets in ratios of 75%, 10%, and 15% respectively, which is commonly used in the context of
clinical datasets.30”
“To assess the stability and significance of the learned features, we first trained 1000 SVM
classifiers on randomly partitioned subsets of the VNS cohort. The mean AUC across models
was significantly greater than that expected under the null distribution (mean AUC = 0.61; t =
28.6, p = 0.001; Fig. 3f), suggesting that the latent representations carried reproducible
predictive signal.”
PET-derived neurotransmitter maps: The description of PET-based receptor/transporter profiles
across nine systems is intriguing. Were these data specifically acquired for this study, or part of a
pre-existing dataset? This is not fully described in the “pretraining data compilation” section.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. The PET-derived neurotransmitter receptor and
transporter maps were not acquired in our cohort, but come from previously published datasets
collated and made available through the neuromaps framework.30 We used these maps to provide
neurochemical context for the model’s salience map, examining the associations across nine
neurotransmitter systems.
“To better understand the biological relevance of the regions in the VQ-VAE model’s salience
map, we studied the associations to the normative chemoarchitecture of the brain using PET-
derived neurotransmitter receptor and transporter expression profiles across nine different
neurotransmitter systems, as compiled from previously published datasets.31,32”
Results / Discussion
The finding of serotonergic large-scale network disruptions is novel and important. However, the
lack of results for the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic system is surprising, given its strong
support in both human (P300, pupillometry) and animal studies (Raedt, Krahl). Could the authors
comment on this apparent discrepancy?
Indeed, the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic (LC-NE) system has been strongly implicated in both
preclinical and human studies of VNS, particularly through its role in arousal regulation, cortical
gain modulation, and event related potential and pupillometric markers of noradrenergic tone.
However, using PET-derived atlases, we did not find a significant alignment between our latent
space and norepinephrine transporter maps (p ~ 0.3). When visualizing and normalizing both
PET maps to a common scale, we found that the NE distribution is concentrated largely within
the brainstem and thalamus (Supplementary Figure 13). Visually, there is some relation to the
salience map, however, this was not significant on spin permutation testing. This may be because
the serotonergic system exhibits a broader, more distributed projection pattern, spanning the
thalamus, striatum, insula, and multiple cortical and subcortical targets. It is possible that the LC-
NE contribution is under-represented in our latent space. The absence of LC-NE findings should
not be interpreted as evidence against noradrenergic involvement in VNS, but the evidence for
serotonergic signalling should highlight its relevance and importance. In the revised manuscript,
we have expanded the discussion on these negative results.
“Fourth, the VQ-VNS model was trained exclusively on T1w imaging. While more advanced
imaging sequences could improve model performance, it would be at the expense of accessibility.
Finally, while our salience maps aligned with the widespread serotonergic system, they did not
overlap with the locus coeruleus-noradrenergic (LC-NE) system. This does not discount the
established mechanistic role of the LC-NE pathway;33 which may be underrepresented within
our latent space due to its highly focal nature (Supplementary Fig. 13). Thus, our findings
highlight the role of widespread serotonergic signaling without precluding the involvement of
the anatomically distinct LC-NE system.”
Supplementary Figure 13. Comparison of PET-derived norepinephrine and serotonin
transporter maps. Norepinephrine transporter distribution shows a highly focal pattern largely
restricted to the brainstem and thalamus. In contrast, serotonin transporter exhibits a more
spatially widespread projection architecture, encompassing striatal, insular, and other
subcortical and cortical regions. Min-max normalized maps highlight the relative difference in
spatial extent. This distinction may contribute to an underrepresentation of noradrenergic
contributions to this current framework.
The statement that “beyond optimal programming, there are no associations between increased
charge density and outcome” (ref 59) may need qualification. Recent work, including Fahoum et
al. (Brain Stimulation, 2022), suggests optimal intensity correlates with outcomes, especially in
pediatric cohorts. Please reconcile with this evidence.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. Within a subset of patients with stimulation parameters
available (n=114), we found no significant difference in stimulation parameters between
responders and non-responders (current: t = -1.2, p = 0.22; duty cycle: t = -1.30, p = 0.20).
Recent analyses indicate that dose matters up to an evidence-based target, after which additional
increases in charge density do not consistently yield further benefit. Very interestingly, our
findings are aligned remarkably well with Fahoum et al. In their population-based study, a group
mean of 1.6 mA and 17.1% duty cycle were associated with greater probability of response. Our
group average current was 1.6 mA and an average duty cycle of 20%. Interestingly, we recently
reported that strong pediatric responders (i.e. “super responders”) to VNS who become seizure-
free tend to do so at very low output currents (Tamura et al., Neuromodulation 2025).
“This study has several limitations. First, while VNS implantation is highly standardized with
minimal inter-subject variability, stimulation parameters were not standardized across sites and
were adjusted at the discretion of the treating clinician, leading to potential differences in the
charge density delivered. However, among participants with available data (N=103), mean
stimulation parameters (output current 1.8mA; duty cycle 20%) were consistent with optimally
programmed populations.26”
Details
The section on region-based morphometry would be clearer if you specify whether this refers to
VBM, SBM, or other approaches.
Region-based morphometric analyses were performed using FreeSurfer-derived estimates of
cortical thickness. We have clarified this detail in the Methods section entitled “Cortical
Thickness Estimation for Lesion Network Network Mapping.”
“Cortical thickness was estimated from T1-weighted images using FreeSurfer as a surface-
based morphometry pipeline to derive individualized thickness maps used in all downstream
atrophy and network-based analyses.”
The statement “region-based morphometry is constrained by atlas-based parcellations…”
requires a proper reference. If reference 15 already supports this, please move it to the end of the
sentence; if not, an additional reference is needed.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. This statement is supported by Guo et al. (2023). In
their study of VNS patients, the authors note that common structural alterations such as cortical
thickness and surface area could not be identified using traditional atlas-based morphometric
approaches at the whole-brain level. They highlight this limitation as motivation for using
deformation-based morphometry, which provides voxel-wise sensitivity to distributed alterations
across the brain. We have clarified this in the revised text by moving the citation to the end of the
sentence.
Conclusion:
In its current form, the manuscript is technically strong and demonstrates the use of highly
specialized methodologies.
However, the presentation may be difficult for clinicians and readers outside the computational field to fully grasp. If the
authors aim for a high-impact journal and a broad audience, we encourage them to simplify and clarify the description of the
methods, and to place greater emphasis on the biological and clinical interpretation of their findings —
particularly the role of the implicated networks and neurotransmitter systems. This would
considerably enhance the accessibility, readability, and overall impact of the work.
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. In response, we have substantially revised the
manuscript to improve accessibility for a broader readership. Specifically, we now clearly state
the goal and rationale behind each technical step, define key methodological terms upon first use,
and include concise synthesis statements throughout to guide interpretation. These revisions
enhance readability and ensure that the biological and clinical relevance of our findings is
emphasized alongside the technical innovation, resulting a more cohesive and broadly accessible
manuscript.
Summary Methodological/Engeneering
The manuscript introduces the VQ-VNS framework, a methodology designed to predict and
classify responses to vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) in pediatric populations. The framework
builds on the VQ-VAE architecture and incorporates interpretability mechanisms by adapting
SHAP and Grad-CAM. Identifying likely responders has the potential to minimize the need for
invasive procedures.
A key limitation of the study is that the proposed methodology is presented with substantial
technical complexity, but with limited benchmarking against alternative approaches.
Major Comments
- The authors reference several alternative approaches for responder identification [11–15]. A
comparative table would help quantify the accuracy improvements of the proposed framework,
particularly in relation to other T1-weighted MRI–based predictive models.
To our knowledge, there are currently no other predictive models of VNS response derived
exclusively from routine T1-weighted MRI. Prior approaches have generally relied on
specialized acquisitions or advanced microstructural metrics. For example, Berger et al. reported
strong performance using diffusion MRI and tractography-based features, which required
extended scan protocols and complex pre-processing pipelines not routinely available in clinical
settings. By contrast, our VQ-VNS framework operates directly on standard clinical T1-weighted
scans, without any additional imaging modalities or advanced preprocessing. Arya et al.
identified clinical correlates of response, such as the absence of a lesion and a longer epilepsy
duration but did not develop an imaging-based predictive model. Our model excluded images
with significant anatomical abnormalities. Other articles either did not report model performance
or did not train a predictive model. We have included below a summary of the cited articles
below.

- The manuscript states: “The resulting archetypal non-responder showed reduced grey matter,
white matter, and subcortical volumes, together with ventricular enlargement.” If such
morphological alterations are discriminative, why would automated segmentation of T1-
weighted images not provide an equally effective classification of responders? A comparison
with standard volumetric and morphometric approaches would strengthen the contribution of the
proposed framework.
While the archetypal reconstructions highlight group-level morphological differences, these
alterations are not consistently present at the level of individual subjects. Indeed, it is the failure
of these models and metrics that inspired the current representation learning approach to VNS
outcome prediction. In the revised manuscript, we have included our analysis of basic imaging-
related metrics using conventional modelling techniques, the inadequacy of which underscores
the superiority of more sophisticated, state-of-the-art techniques like VQ-VNS. These findings
are concordant with the central thesis of the paper, which is that latent space representations
based on generative models designed to learn compact representations of brain patterns are
required to understand complex associations outcomes to VNS.
Informed by differences highlighted by the archetypal reconstructions, we trained both a logistic
regression model and a support vector machine using automated segmentation of T1-weighted
images alone. These models, trained exclusively on FreeSurfer-derived gray matter, white
matter, subcortical gray matter, and ventricular volumes, demonstrated near chance performance
(logistic regression: AUC = 0.49; SVM: AUC = 0.55) in predicting VNS response. This suggests
that, individually, automatically segmented features on T1w imaging are not on their own
predictive of response. The strength of the proposed framework lies in its ability to learn internal
latent representations that capture subtle, distributed, and non-linear structural features across the
cohort. These features are not easily detectable through conventional volumetric or
morphometric pipelines. While the differences between archetypal responders and non-
responders helps to explain some of the characteristics that may drive classification, they are
insufficient to enable classification on an individual subject level.
- The original spin permutation procedure rotated cortical surface maps while preserving
contralateral symmetry. Was this constraint maintained in the present experiments? Furthermore,
the original test statistic excluded non-cortical regions. Were such regions incorporated in the
current analysis? These methodological details require clarification.
Our approach was inspired by the originally described spin permutation framework35 but was not
identical in implementation. Instead of applying surface-based rotations, we implemented a 3D
rotational affine transformation directly to the latent brain volumes. This procedure preserves the
relative spatial arrangement of all voxels (i.e., no voxel-wise shuffling is performed), thereby
maintaining bilateral or contralateral symmetries present in the data. Additionally, our
implementation of spin permutation includes both cortical and subcortical structures. This
broader inclusion was intentional, as our latent representation captures patterns beyond just the
cerebral cortex.
Minor Comments
- The statement that prognostic signatures are “likely embedded in subtle, distributed, and
nonlinear anatomical patterns” would benefit from supporting references.
Thank you for allowing us to clarify this claim. Prior studies that have successfully predicted
VNS outcomes using advanced neuroimaging (e.g. diffusion tensor imaging, functional MRI,
magneotencephalography, etc.), as in (Berger et al., 2024; Ibrahim et al., 2017; Mithani et al.,
2019), have all identified subtle, distributed features predictive of response. Furthermore, most of
them have used non-linear modelling for classification. Conversely, studies that have tried to use
gross anatomical features for VNS prediction have had limited success. As such, we propose
that, based on these prior works, predictive features on anatomical imaging are also likely to be
subtle, distributed, and non-linear. We have added citations to this claim now.
- The rationale for selecting an SVM classifier should be expanded, in comparison with other
machine learning methods (e.g., random forests, k-nearest neighbors).
Our choice of SVM as the classifier for the learned embeddings was guided by both theoretical
considerations and empirical evaluation. Among several standard classifiers tested, including
logistic regression, random forest, and k-nearest neighbors (kNN), SVM consistently provided
the best balance between model complexity, robustness to overfitting, and predictive accuracy on
held-out data. Logistic regression tended to underfit, random forests showed overfitting
tendencies, and kNN performed less favorably overall.
These comparisons are now presented in Supplementary Figure 7 which confirms that SVM
achieved the highest classification accuracy for the learned latent representations. Together,
these results support its selection as the final classifier in the VQ-VNS framework.

The composite loss function we adopted was based on Tudosiu et al., 2024, where the authors
performed extensive ablation experiments to evaluate the contribution of each loss component.
As this prior work has already rigorously demonstrated the necessity and impact of each term,
we did not repeat these ablations here.
We have included this detail under “Self-supervised representation learning captures anatomical
patterns associated with VNS outcome” in the Results:
“The composite loss function we adopted was based on prior experiments43 where extensive
ablations were performed to evaluate the contribution of each loss component.”
- The claim that “the model’s reconstructions preserved fine anatomical details” appears
somewhat contradictory, since VQ-VAE models are known to lose fine-scale structural
information. A more precise description of which features are preserved or lost would enhance
interpretability.
Thank you for allowing us to clarify this point. Our implementation was explicitly evaluated for
anatomical fidelity using a multi-modal set of metrics. As detailed in the section entitled “Self-
supervised representation learning captures anatomical patterns associated with VNS outcome,”
we quantified reconstruction fidelity with MS-SSIM, FID, and MSE, and further assessed
anatomical plausibility through structure-wise correlations after SynthSeg segmentation. These
analyses demonstrated that the model preserved key anatomical details, with correlations across
tissue classes ranging from 0.96 to 1.00. Although reconstruction fidelity was somewhat lower in
subjects with pronounced structural abnormalities, overall performance remained high,
consistent with training on predominantly anatomically typical brains. Our claim is therefore
specific to the present implementation, supported by the reported metrics.
- The observation that “reconstruction fidelity was lower in subjects with significant structural
abnormalities” raises the question of whether this reduction affects classification performance.
Are response predictions less reliable for patients with pronounced abnormalities?
The VQ-VAE was pretrained exclusively on brains without significant structural abnormalities,
which explains the lower reconstruction fidelity observed in cases with pronounced structural
abnormalities. To avoid introducing systematic biases, patients with major abnormalities were
excluded from the classification analyses. As a result, the reduction in reconstruction fidelity in
subjects with significant structural abnormalities would not have biased classifier performance.
- Additionally, the reconstruction fidelity of the CONNECTiVOS pediatric epilepsy cohort
should be reported.

text (thalami, brainstem, insular cortex, peri-Rolandic regions). How were the reported regions

For interpretability, we focused our description on regions corresponding to the vagus afferent

responsiveness43. All regions highlighted meet a minimum threshold of 0.30 on a 0-0.5 log scale,

Given the subtle differences between the images, we provided a quantitative comparison in the
accompanying bar plot, which more clearly highlight the volumetric distinctions between the
archetypal responder and archetypal non-responder. To avoid confusion, we have revised the

volumes across four tissue classes in the pretraining test set, demonstrating high reconstruction fidelity.
(c) Representative reconstruction of a subject with a previous resection from the CONNECTiVOS cohort.
(d) Synthetic images of the archetypal VNS responder and non-responder reconstructed from the latent
space using the VQ-VAE decoder. Differences are subtle and not visually apparent. (e) The synthetic

trained using hold-out cross validation perform significantly better than chance. (g) Receiver operating

temporal lobectomy (AUC = 0.57, p =0.12).

(5-HTT) expression”. Can you quantify this result?Clarification is needed.
We found that the concentration of model attention within the brain was enriched in serotonin
transporter (5-HTT) expression based on normative PET data. This was quantified by computing
the correlation between attention weights and regional 5-HTT density. The correlation
coefficient and corresponding p-value are more explicitly denoted in the revised results.
“We generated 1,000 such null maps per comparison to compute empirical p-values and account
for spatial autocorrelation. The VQ-VAE’s attention was concentrated within brain regions
enriched in serotonin transporter (5-HTT) expression (r = 0.26, p = 0.04; Fig. 4b).”
- “To assess the predictive value of clinical data, a support vector machine (SVM) was trained on
80% of the dataset (discovery cohort, n = 550) to predict VNS outcome, with the remaining 20%
held out for validation (n = 144)”. Was there an independent test set? Clarification is needed.
In our analysis of the predictive value of clinical features, the SVM was trained exclusively on
the 80% training set. The remaining 20% was never used during model development and was
held out as an independent test set to evaluate performance after training was complete. We have
revised the text to clarify this distinction.
“To assess the predictive value of clinical data, a support vector machine (SVM) was trained on
80% of the dataset (n = 550) to predict VNS outcome. The remaining 20% (n = 144) was held
out as an independent test set to evaluate model performance after training.”
- “Structure-wise agreement was evaluated across four tissue classes – grey matter, white matter,
subcortical grey matter, and ventricles – by computing the Pearson correlation between
reconstructed and original volumes across subjects”. This only accounts for the volume size of
each tissue type and not their location. Adding the DICE scores or an equivalent would
provide a more comprehensive assessment.
We have now computed Dice similarity coefficients between the reconstructed and original
tissue maps for each class. The results show high agreement across tissue classes, consistent with

were endpoints chosen instead of complete streamlines?
Endpoints were chosen instead of complete streamlines because our objective was to map direct
structural disconnections resulting from regional atrophy, rather than to characterize entire
trajectories. Full streamlines often traverse multiple white-matter regions and are susceptible to
gyral bias and false continuations, making them less specific to true cortical terminations.44

approach has been used in prior structural connectivity studies29.

Thank you for this suggestion. A visualization of the cortical atrophy map was provided in

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Implantable neurotechnologies are increasingly used to reduce seizure burden in epilepsy. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), the most common option, is effective for only half of patients, with no means to predict outcome prior to surgery. As a result, many children undergo invasive and costly procedures without benefit. Although T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (T1w) is routinely acquired presurgically and may capture structural brain differences relevant to treatment outcome, its high dimensionality relative to sample sizes has limited its utility in predictive modeling. To address this challenge, we present VQ-VNS, a deep representation learning model to predict VNS outcome based on preoperative T1w (n=263). First, we present data from the largest pediatric VNS cohort (n=1046), wherein presurgical clinical data could not predict response (AUC 0.54,p>0.99). Next, VQ-VNS was pretrained on 7433 T1w images to learn compact anatomical representations enabling its classifier to predict VNS response (AUC=0.73,p=0.007). Model predictions localized to serotonin-rich brain regions and inferred large-scale disruptions in network connectivity among non-responders. This biologically-interpretable predictor based on routine structural imaging improves upon current clinical decision-making.

---

## Introduction

Epilepsy is the most common serious neurological disorder in children.1 The medical and psychosocial burden of drug-resistant epilepsy2 (DRE) has driven the increased usage of implantable neurotechnologies to improve seizure control. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is the most commonly recommended device,3 supported by decades of clinical experience in pediatric populations. VNS has been shown to reduce seizure frequency,4 improve quality of life,5 and decrease mortality.2 However, only half of patients realize a benefit after treatment, and clinicians are currently unable to identify responders to VNS prior to surgery,6–8 leading to unnecessary, invasive, and costly procedures. Given that there is little variability in implantation technique,9 heterogenous outcomes are likely related to intrinsic differences among patients – particularly in brain structure and function. There is an unmet need to presurgically identify responders to VNS to personalize treatment options.

T1-weighted (T1w) MRI, a routine component of presurgical evaluation in pediatric epilepsy,10 represents a high-dimensional feature space ( R > 6 million voxels per image) that may contain complex, prognostically-relevant biomarkers. However, it remains underutilized in predictive modelling, as prognostic signatures are likely embedded in subtle, distributed, and nonlinear anatomical patterns11–13 – challenges compounded by the modest sample sizes typical of pediatric imaging datasets. Approaches to identify VNS responders based on coarse imaging features such as the presence of lesions14,15 or structural etiologies of epilepsy15–17 have not been informative and reported inconsistent associations. Region-based morphometry,18 is constrained by atlas-based parcellations that fail to capture diffuse, whole-brain patterns and yields weak associations with outcome. Crucially, there are no studies that have developed predictive models for VNS response on an individual patient level that are suitable for clinical use.8 Consequently, structural imaging has yet to be adopted as a viable predictor of VNS response.

Recent advances in generative modelling have enabled self-supervised learning of compact whole-brain embeddings from high-dimensional imaging data, capturing subtle and distributed anatomical patterns without reliance on predefined features. Architectures such as vector-quantized variational autoencoders19 (VQ-VAEs) and latent diffusion models20 have leveraged these lower dimensional representations to synthesize realistic brain images while modelling interindividual variability.21,22 While primarily developed for image synthesis, these models' principal utility in clinical contexts lies in their ability to learn compressed, semantically rich representations of whole-brain anatomy. Yet, their application to clinical prediction tasks remains underexplored.23 Moreover, most prior work has focused on adult datasets – such as the UK BioBank24 – with limited attention to pediatric populations despite their increased neurodevelopmental variability.25

In addition to technical barriers, clinical deployment of deep learning in neuroimaging is often limited by clinician apprehension about model opacity. Interpretability is increasingly viewed as a prerequisite for clinical adoption.26 Consequently, there is growing interest in addressing this requirement by either developing inherently interpretable models or applying post hoc analyses to explain the outputs of models not explicitly designed for interpretability.27 In the context of implantable neurotechnologies, where treatment decisions often involve surgical risk and uncertainty, predictive models must offer both accuracy and mechanistic transparency, grounded in neurobiological plausibility.

In this work, we present VQ-VNS, a clinically focused deep learning framework for predicting response to VNS directly from presurgical T1w MRI. Our approach combines a VQ-VAE, trained to learn discrete whole-brain anatomical representations, followed by a linear support vector machine28 (SVM) classifier for outcome prediction. To provide interpretability, we integrate gradient-weighted class activation mapping29 (Grad-CAM) and Shapley additive explanations30 (SHAP) to generate voxel-level predictive salience maps. To examine the neurobiological mechanisms underlying model performance, we also related the salience maps to normative neurochemical brain architectures as well as large-scale brain networks disrupted in non-responders using normative connectomic data. Our results demonstrate that interpretable deep representation learning can be leveraged to predict VNS outcomes while offering insight into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying treatment response.

---

## Results

Clinical data do not predict response after VNS
We compiled the largest database of children to undergo VNS (n = 1046) from 11 North American centers through the Connectomics and Vagus Nerve Stimulation Outcome Study (CONNECTiVOS, Fig. 1a).28 Participants were deemed responders if seizure frequency was reduced by ≥80% and non-responders if ≤20% (n = 694, Fig. 1b) to reflect the bimodal distribution of seizure outcomes and mitigate the effects of ambiguous intermediate outcomes.29 The mean [SD; range] age was 10.6 [4.7; 0.8-24.2] years, 54% male and included 51% responders (Fig. 1b-c). This age range was included to capture the full developmental trajectory of brain maturation amongst pediatric and young adult populations that undergo VNS.

We first examined the association of each presurgical clinical variable with response by applying ordinary least squares regression (Fig. 1d; Supplementary Fig. 1). No clinical features were significantly associated with VNS outcome after false discovery rate correction (Supplementary Table 1). Nonlinear embedding of the clinical data using uniform manifold approximation and projection31 (UMAP) also failed to separate responders and non-responders (Fig. 1e; s = –2.7 × 10-4, p = 0.71), which was also corroborated by principal component analysis which revealed low explained variance (<12% for PC1) and no systematic response associated differences (Supplementary Fig. 2, Supplementary Table 2). Labelling the UMAP embeddings by treatment site revealed visually apparent but objectively weak (s = –0.04, p > 0.99) site-specific groupings (Fig. 1f), indicative of subtle inter-site variability in patient selection criteria without strong site-level effects.

Finally, consistent with findings in smaller cohorts,6,8 an SVM model trained on presurgical clinical features – including demographics, epilepsy history, and electroencephalography – was unable to distinguish responders to VNS from non-responders beyond chance-level performance (AUC = 0.54, p > 0.99; Fig. 1g). Furthermore, there was no difference in output current (1.9  0.7 vs. 1.7  0.7; t(101) = -1.4; p = 0.17; n = 103) or duty cycle (21  10% vs. 19  10%; t(101) = -1.3, p = 0.2, n = 103) between responders and non-responders.

Self-supervised representation learning captures anatomical patterns associated with VNS outcome
To study whether structural brain differences could predict outcome, we developed VQ-VNS, a deep representation learning model to identify VNS responders based on standard T1w sequences (Fig. 2). Because each T1w MRI scan contains over six million voxels – far exceeding the sample sizes of most pediatric epilepsy datasets (typically < 100 patients per center)32 – dimensionality reduction is critical to mitigate overfitting and enable effective model training. However, conventional approaches to dimensionality reduction, such as region-based parcellation, are insufficient to model the relationship between structural alterations and response following VNS (Supplementary Tables 3-4). Thus, the VQ-VNS model consists of two stages: 1) a VQ-VAE19 architecture compresses the high-dimensional MRI data into a compact latent representation, and (2) a support vector machine (SVM) classifies patients based on these latent features. The VQ-VAE architecture is well suited to compressing complex anatomical data into compact latent representations.21 We trained this model on large datasets of healthy subjects and persons with epilepsy who had not received VNS (n = 7,433; Fig. 2a–c). These datasets included participants across the lifespan (age 1.9 - 88.9 years) and contained a wide range of anatomical and acquisition-related variability to support the VQ-VAE’s ability to learn robust, generalizable representations. We optimized the VQ-VAE model with a composite loss term – comprising mean absolute error, perceptual loss,33 spectral loss34, commitment loss19 and an adversarial term derived from a discriminator35 model – to generate high-quality reconstructions of the input T1w image. This composite loss function was based on prior experiments21 where extensive ablations were performed to evaluate the contribution of each loss component.

The VQ-VAE’s reconstructions preserved anatomical details and captured biologically meaningful variation (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Fig. 3). We evaluated reconstruction fidelity using established metrics, including multiscale structural similarity36 (MS-SSIM), Fréchet Inception Distance37 (FID), and mean squared error (MSE). The VQ-VAE demonstrated strong performance (Supplementary Table 5), with a mean (SD) MS-SSIM of 0.97 (0.01), FID of 1.5 × 10-3 (1.2 × 10-3), and an MSE of 3.7 × 10-3 (8.6 × 10-4). To assess anatomical plausibility, we segmented both original and reconstructed images using SynthSeg38 and computed structure-wise correlations and Dice-Sørensen coefficients across four tissue classes: grey matter, white matter, subcortical grey matter, and ventricles. The VQ-VAE reconstructions demonstrated high correlation with true volumes across all four classes, with Pearson correlation coefficients ranging from 0.96 to 1.00 (Fig. 3b); furthermore, the reconstructions exhibited strong spatial overlap, yielding mean Dice-Sørensen coefficients ranging from 0.78 to 0.91 (Supplementary Table 6). Reconstruction fidelity was lower in subjects with significant structural abnormalities (Fig. 3a; Supplementary Fig. 4) with a mean (SD) SSIM of 0.95 (0.01), FID of 4.1 × 10-3 (9.8 × 10-4), and MSE of 4.7 × 10-3 (9.2 × 10-3), consistent with the VQ-VAE being trained primarily on anatomically typical brains.

Finally, we assessed whether this learned latent space captured features associated with VNS response without additional training. We encoded each subject’s image from the training subset of children who underwent VNS in the CONNECTiVOS cohort (199 of 263 images, Supplementary Fig. 5), computed the median latent representations separately for responders and non-responders, quantized these representations, and decoded them to generate synthetic archetypal brains (Fig. 3c). Compared to the archetypal responder, the resulting archetypal non-responder showed reduced grey matter, white matter and subcortical volumes, together with ventricular enlargement (Fig. 3d). These differences suggest that the latent representations captured structural features relevant to treatment outcome without direct optimization for VNS outcome prediction and that VNS non-responders exhibit lower brain volumes (i.e. atrophy) compared to responders.

Latent representations support accurate prediction and spatial interpretation of VNS outcome
To evaluate the predictive utility of the latent space for response following VNS, we trained a linear SVM classifier (Fig. 2e) using quantized latent vectors from the frozen VQ-VAE encoder. To reduce dimensionality, each four-dimensional latent tensor (x, y, and z spatial dimensions × feature channels) was spatially averaged across the x, y, and z axes, yielding a single 32-dimensional21 feature vector per subject. Each element of this vector therefore captures the global magnitude of the respective latent feature learned from the underlying T1w image. We then applied two-sided t-test-based feature selection on the training data (n = 199) to retain 27 of the 32 latent features (Supplementary Table 7), which were used to train the SVM, which demonstrated the strongest predictive performance among multiple classifiers (Supplementary Fig. 6). To assess the stability and significance of the learned features, we first trained 1000 SVM classifiers on randomly partitioned subsets of the VNS cohort. The mean AUC across models was significantly greater than that expected under the null distribution (mean AUC = 0.61; t(1998) = 28.6, p = 1e-150; Fig. 3e), suggesting that the latent representations carried measurable predictive signal.

We then trained a final SVM classifier using the training (n = 199) and validation (n = 25) subsets of the VNS cohort and tested on an independent held-out set (n = 39). The resulting model achieved an AUC of 0.73 in predicting response to VNS (permutation p = 0.007; Fig. 3f; Supplementary Fig. 7; Supplementary Table 8). The model maintained its predictive capacity across diverse age groups and treatment centers (Supplementary Fig. 7C). Model performance remained robust with the inclusion of subjects with ambiguous outcomes binarized at the 50% seizure reduction threshold (n = 53; AUC = 0.67, permutation p = 0.02; Supplementary Fig. 8). To evaluate the classifier’s ability to generalize across acquisition sites, we performed site hold-out validation, in which all images from one site were excluded during training and used exclusively for testing (Supplementary Table 9). Sites contributing small sample sizes were combined to create a single evaluation set. The classifiers achieved above chance accuracy (0.61 to 0.67), suggesting site-invariant structural features predictive of VNS response.

To evaluate the specificity of the SVM to predicting VNS outcomes, we tested its performance on an independent cohort of children who underwent temporal lobectomy for temporal lobe epilepsy39 (n = 102; mean age [SD] = 12.8 [3.9] years; 69.6% seizure freedom). The SVM model did not predict outcomes above chance level after temporal lobectomy (AUC = 0.57, permutation p = 0.12; Fig. 3f), suggesting that its decision boundary did not generalize to this population.

To visualize brain regions contributing most to model predictions, we implemented a hybrid salience attribution method integrating SHAP30 values from the SVM with Grad-CAM29 from the VQ-VAE encoder. Subject-specific SHAP values corresponding to the 27 selected latent features were expanded to a full 32-dimensional vector by assigning zeros to the unselected features. We computed the dot product between this SHAP vector and each subject’s latent representation, and backpropagated the resulting scalar through the VQ-VAE encoder. Gradients and activations were then extracted from the final convolutional layer to produce voxel-wise salience maps. This approach enabled SVM-derived feature importance to guide spatial salience attribution in the original image space. We identified several regions of high predictive value including the thalami, brainstem, and peri-Rolandic regions (Fig. 4a).

Model salience localizes to serotonergic networks disrupted in VNS non-responders
To better understand how model predictions relate to the chemoarchitecture of the brain, we correlated the VQ-VAE model’s salience map to the topology of brain receptor and transporter densities across nine different neurotransmitter systems from over 1200 healthy individuals.40 Neurotransmitter receptors are heterogeneously distributed across the neocortex and may be modulated by implanted technologies to modify neural states and reshape network-level communication.41 Each correlation was assessed against a null distribution generated via spin permutation testing, in which a single rotational affine was applied across all subjects’ latent salience maps for each permutation, prior to upscaling and averaging (Fig. 4b). We generated 1,000 such null maps per comparison to compute empirical p-values and account for spatial autocorrelation. The VQ-VAE’s attention was concentrated within brain regions enriched in serotonin transporter (5-HTT) expression (r = 0.26, p = 0.04; Fig. 4c).

The anatomically distributed pattern of salient regions also suggested involvement of broader brain networks in VNS response. To further interpret model predictions, we leveraged lesion network mapping, an approach which links focal structural abnormalities to disruptions in large-scale brain circuitry using normative connectomic data.42 This allowed us to test whether brain atrophy in non-responders, relative to 2,382 typically developing children (age 1.9 to 25.0 years, 63% male), converged upon a common network aligned with the VQ-VNS model’s saliency profile. We first demonstrated that cortical thickness measurements did not contain site-specific batch effects (Supplementary Fig. 9) and that group-level spatial patterns of atrophy alone did not clearly distinguish responders from non-responders (Supplementary Fig. 10). Regional brain atrophy maps converged upon large-scale structural (Fig. 4d, Supplementary Fig. 11) and functional (Fig. 4e) networks that were preferentially disrupted in non-responders to VNS. The VQ-VNS model’s saliency map showed significant spatial concordance (Supplementary Fig. 12a) with these structural (p<0.001, Supplementary Fig. 12b) and functional (p=0.04, Supplementary Fig. 12c) networks following spin permutation tests. Network findings were also concordant with brain regions to which vagus afferent fibres are known to project through the nucleus tractus solitarius,32 including areas that are activated by VNS.43

## Methods

VNS Data Collection
Data were collected through a multi-institutional registry as part of the CONNECTiVOS study (Connectomic profiling and Vagus nerve stimulation Outcomes Study).59 This study involved children with epilepsy and was conducted across multiple North American sites, with local investigators engaged in design, data collection, and authorship. This study was approved by the institutional review boards of all participating sites (REB Approval Number 1000060282PID) and carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.60 Data were collected from 1046 patients who underwent VNS implantation at centers in Canada and the United States. Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are described in the CONNECTiVOS protocol. All data were collected under local ethics approval with informed consent and assent where appropriate, and were de-identified prior to analysis. No material transfer, resource-poor settings, or elevated researcher risk were involved. We did not prespecify indications for VNS implantation, and all programming parameters were at the discretion of treating physicians.

For each participant, we collected continuous data on age at VNS implantation, duration of epilepsy, and percent seizure reduction at last follow-up based on parent-reported seizure frequency. Binary variables included: sex, presence of a genetic diagnosis, developmental delay, family history of epilepsy, history of infantile spasms, congenital or acquired epilepsy etiology, and prior epilepsy surgery. EEG data included variables indicating focal versus generalized seizure onset and lateralization of interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs). Preoperative imaging data including High-resolution 3D T1-weighted (T1w) were collected both prospectively and retrospectively.

T1w MRI for the VNS cohort were acquired at either 1.5T or 3T. Scanner manufacturers include Philips, Siemens, General Electric, and Toshiba. Scanner models included Achieva, Skyra, Trio TIM, Ingenuity, Signa HDxt, Discovery MR750, Ingenia, Intera, Symphony, Prisma, Avanto, Signa Excite, Symphony TIM, Trio, Titan, Discovery MR750w, and Genesis Signa. Key parameters for T1-weighted imaging were: flip angle, 12.3° (8.0° – 40.0°); echo time, 3.7 ms (1.7 – 9.2 ms); repetition time, 7.9 ms (1.1 – 25.0 ms); and mean voxel size, 0.7x0.7x0.7mm.

Pretraining Data Compilation
We compiled data from a cohort of healthy subjects and persons with epilepsy from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE, n = 412),61 the Healthy Brain Network (HBN, n = 2081),62 the Calgary Preschool MRI (n = 265),63 the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN, n = 649),64 and the Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC, n = 923),65 SickKids internal normative dataset (n = 1260), The Imaging Database for Epilepsy And Surgery (IDEAS, n = 542),66 Focal Cortical Dysplasia Type II (FCD-2, n = 170),67 Temporal Lobe Epilepsy – UNAM (UNAM-TLE, n = 66), Human Connectome Project Young Adult (HCP, n = 1065)68 datasets for a combined dataset of 7433 images. To balance retaining a sufficient training set size with sufficient subjects for validation and robust assessment on a held-out test cohort, these data were split into training, validation and test sets in ratios of 75%, 10%, and 15% respectively, which is commonly used in the context of clinical datasets

The SickKids internal normative T1w images were acquired at either 1.5T or 3T across various scanners (Signa HDxt, GE Healthcare; Achieva, Philips Healthcare; Magnetom Skyra, Siemens Healthineers) with a dedicated head-coil. Images were acquired either in the sagittal or the axial plane: TR/TE, 6-9/2-5 ms; flip angle: 10-15 degrees, mean voxel size, 1.0x1.0x1.5 mm.

All T1w images were brain extracted,38,69 70resampled to 1mm3 isotropic resolution,71, bias field corrected, intensity normalized with Fuzzy C-means,72 and rigidly registered73 to a 1mm MNI brain extracted template (Fig. 2a).74

Analysis of clinical data
Participants were classified as non-responders if they had ≤20% seizure frequency reduction, and as responders for ≥80% seizure frequency reduction based on the bimodal distribution of treatment outcomes (Fig. 1b) and to mitigate misclassification risk inherent to seizure reporting from participants with ambiguous outcomes.75 Based on the outcome threshold, 694 of the 1046 subjects were included. We used ordinary least squares regression to model the univariable relationship between each clinical variable and VNS response. Counts of missing values for each clinical variable are presented in Supplementary Table 10. False discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied to adjust for multiple comparisons.

To model multivariable and non-linear relationships, we applied Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP).31 Silhouette scores76 quantified the clustering quality of UMAP embeddings by outcome and site, with significance assessed via one-sided one-sample t-tests. To further assess whether the observed manifold structure reflected biologically or methodologically meaningful variance, we additionally performed principal component analysis (PCA) on the same dataset. Loadings of the top principal components were examined to identify the metrics contributing most to overall variance within the clinical data. Scores for the leading components were then compared between responders and non-responders to evaluate whether these reduced dimensions captured differences associated with VNS outcome.

To assess the predictive value of clinical data, a support vector machine (SVM)36 was trained on 80% of the dataset (n = 550) to predict VNS outcome. The remaining 20% (n = 144) was held out as an independent test set to evaluate model performance after training. To ensure that both training and test sets contained only clearly defined responders and non-responders, subjects with ambiguous (intermediate) outcomes were excluded prior to this split. Recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV)77 was employed for feature selection. The clinical SVM model’s performance was quantified using area under the curve (AUC) and confusion matrices. We additionally evaluated model performance with the inclusion of subjects with ambiguous outcomes (n = 352) and observed no improvement.

Cortical Thickness Estimation and Regional-based Modelling of Response
Cortical thickness was estimated from T1-weighted images using FreeSurfer71 to derive individualized thickness maps used in all downstream atrophy and network-based analyses. Cortical surface reconstruction in FreeSurfer v7.4.2 began with an affine transformation aligning images to the MNI305 atlas, followed by B1 bias field estimation from white matter intensity variations and subsequent intensity inhomogeneity correction. Intensity normalization was then performed to correct for cross-site and cross-scanner fluctuations that would otherwise disrupt subsequent intensity-based segmentation steps. The skull was stripped, and white matter boundaries were automatically identified based on intensity and neighbour constraints. The white matter surface then underwent smoothing through tessellation and was expanded outwards to identify the boundaries of the pial surface. Cortical thickness was calculated as the average distance from a point on the smoothed white matter surface to its corresponding point on the pial surface and vice versa. The surfaces and parametric maps were spherically inflated and registered to a standard spherical atlas.78 This was followed by region-wise regression to VNS outcome with a generalized linear model accounting for age and estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV). The parcellations were derived from the Desikan-Killiany Atlas. Although this pipeline was established in adults, it has been validated for use in children,79 and all surface reconstructions were visually examined for accuracy.

Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoder
T1-weighted MRI scans are inherently high-dimensional, making it challenging to train predictive models directly on raw voxel intensities – particularly in the context of relatively small clinical imaging datasets. This necessitates an approach to represent these data in a low dimensional space without loss of detail necessary for downstream classification tasks. We implemented a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE)19 from the MONAI library to generate these lower dimensional latent representations. Compared to classical convolutional classifiers that require pretraining on surrogate labels such as age or diagnosis, using an autoencoder allowed the model to learn representations based solely on structural anatomy, without bias toward any specific pretraining objective.
