Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoder Implementation
The input to the VQ-VAE model was a 3D volume of size 176 × 208 × 176. The encoder comprised four convolutional downsampling blocks with 128, 128, 256, and 256 feature maps, respectively, yielding a latent representation of size 11 × 13 × 11 with 32 channels. Quantization was performed using a codebook with 2,048 entries and embedding dimension 32. The resulting quantized latent had the same shape as the encoded latent. The decoder consisted of four transposed convolutional layers to reconstruct the final image.

The discriminator was a PatchDiscriminator from MONAI, consisting of four convolutional layers with 64 channels each, followed by a classifier head with a single output channel. Training was performed for 140 epochs using the Adam optimizer83 with a learning rate of 1e-5. The generator used 𝛽 = (0.9, 0.999), and the discriminator used 𝛽 = (0.5, 0.99). Gradient loss terms were weighted by empirically selected scaling factors: 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0, and 1.0 for ℒ ,ℒ ,ℒ ,ℒ and ℒ respectively. Training was conducted on a single node in the SickKids High Performance Computing cluster with an Nvidia H100 NVL GPU (96 GB VRAM), 18 CPU cores and 48 GB of RAM.

Reconstruction Quality Evaluation
To evaluate the fidelity of VQ-VAE reconstructions, we computed three complementary image-level metrics – mean squared error (MSE), multiscale structural similarity (MS-SSIM),36 and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID)37 between the original and the reconstructed 3D T1-weighted images. MSE and MS-SSIM were computed using MONAI (MSEMetric, MultiScaleSSIMMetric), and FID was calculated using features extracted from a pretrained ResNet-50 model,84 following global average pooling across spatial dimensions. To assess the VQ-VAE model’s robustness to anatomical abnormalities, we performed a secondary evaluation on 106 subjects with abnormal imaging findings. Reconstruction fidelity was evaluated using the same three metrics – MSE, MS-SSIM, and FID.

To assess anatomical plausibility, all reconstructed and original images were segmented using SynthSeg.38 Structure-wise agreement was evaluated across four tissue classes – grey matter, white matter, subcortical grey matter, and ventricles – by computing the Pearson correlation between reconstructed and original volumes across subjects.

Training the SVM Classifier to Predict VNS Response
Response classification used the same thresholds as applied to the clinical data: ≥80% seizure reduction for responders and ≤20% for non-responders. Subjects with significant anomalies, prior neurosurgical intervention (Supplementary Fig. 4a-d), or conflicting outcome assessments, were excluded. After filtering, the final dataset comprised 263 subjects (Supplementary Fig. 5). The 263 patients included in model training did not differ significantly from the excluded cohort in terms of demographic or clinical characteristics (Supplementary Table 12).

An SVM classifier was trained on vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent embeddings to predict binary treatment outcomes. The VQ-VAE first encoded T1-weighted MRI scans into a compressed latent representation, which was averaged across its spatial dimensions and flattened to yield a one-dimensional 32 feature vector per subject.

Latent features were evaluated via two-sided t-tests, and only those showing significant group-level differences (p < 0.05) were retained (27 of 32, Supplementary Table 7). To assess the stability and significance of the learned features, we first trained 1000 SVM classifiers with class balancing and a high regularization parameter (C=5000) on randomly partitioned subsets of the VNS cohort. To assess generalizability, a final SVM was trained with a training, validation set, and held-out test set. To minimize data imbalance, participants were split into training (n = 199, responders = 100, non-responders = 99), validation (n = 25, responders = 13, non-responders = 12), and held-out test sets (n = 39, responders = 19, non-responders = 20) using stratified sampling to preserve approximately equal proportions of responders and non-responders in each subset. Model performance was evaluated using area under the curve (AUC) and confusion matrices across these sets. Robustness was assessed by permutation testing with 1,000 label shuffles to generate a null distribution of AUC scores, enabling empirical significance estimation. This procedure tests whether the VQ-VNS model’s observed performance exceeds chance expectations, thereby confirming that predictions reflect a learned mapping between input features and outcome.

To evaluate the SVM classifier’s ability to generalize across acquisition sites, we performed site-hold-out validation, in which all images from one site were excluded during training and used exclusively for test. To enable evaluation of smaller test sizes, sites were grouped by geographic region. To further assess robustness, we tested the VQ-VNS model’s performance in subjects with intermediate outcomes - seizure reductions between 20% and 80% - without further model training. For this analysis response was binarized at the conventional >50% threshold. Similarly, model performance was evaluated using AUC and confusion matrices. The VQ-VAE encoder was frozen during SVM training. Latent embeddings were generated using an Nvidia RTX A6000 (Ampere, 48 GB VRAM) GPU, after which SVM training and inference were performed on CPU. In inference mode – including VQ-VAE latent generation and SVM prediction – the average runtime per subject was 0.19 seconds.

To evaluate the specificity of the VQ-VNS model’s performance, we tested its ability to predict seizure freedom in a separate cohort of patients with temporal lobe epilepsy39 (TLE) who underwent temporal lobectomy (n = 102; mean age [SD] = 12.8 [3.9] years; 69.6% seizure freedom). This retrospective TLE cohort was selected because high-quality preoperative T1-weighted imaging and detailed postoperative outcome data were available, enabling an assessment of whether the VQ-VNS model, training exclusively on VNS recipients, generalizes to an independent surgical population. In this cohort, approximately 70% of patients achieved seizure freedom following surgery, which enabled the evaluation of model specificity. T1-weighted images were acquired using Philips and GE scanners (Achieva, Genesis Signa, Signa HDxt, Signa Excite) with field strengths of 1.5T or 3T. Imaging parameters were: flip angle = 13.6° (range: 8.0°–30.0°), echo time = 4.3 ms (2.3–4.6 ms), repetition time = 8.7 ms (5.0–25.0 ms), and mean voxel size = 0.9 × 0.9 × 1.4 mm. Images with gross abnormalities were excluded as was performed in the VNS cohort.

Model Interpretation Using Gradient-based Salience Mapping
To identify brain regions relevant for outcome prediction, we generated voxel-wise heatmaps using a hybrid approach inspired by both Shapley additive explanations85 (SHAP) and gradient-weighted class activation mapping29 (Grad-CAM). The VQVAE encoded each subject’s image into its quantized latent representation. The feature vector for each subject was passed to the trained SVM to predict response. SHAP values were then computed using a model-agnostic explainer with the median training feature vector as the reference. For each subject, the resulting SHAP vector was used in a dot product with their input feature vector. This scalar output was backpropagated through the encoder, and gradients were extracted from the final convolutional layer to generate latent salience maps based on gradient-weighted activations.

The latent salience maps were upsampled to the original image resolution and then spatially normalized to MNI space by applying the subject-specific nonlinear transformation from model T1 space to MNI space, previously estimated using ANTs.86 Individual maps were averaged across all subjects, and the resulting group-level salience map was converted to absolute values to reflect feature importance. The signed average salience map was retained for receptor and transporter expression analyses, which are sensitive to the direction of feature contributions. Visualizations of the salience map are log transformed to aid in identification of the most salient regions.

Mapping neurotransmitter receptor expression within salience map
To better understand the biological relevance of the regions in the VQ-VAE model’s salience map, we studied the associations to the normative chemoarchitecture of the brain using PET-derived neurotransmitter receptor and transporter expression profiles across nine different neurotransmitter systems, as compiled from previously published datasets.87 These datasets were acquired from over 1200 healthy individuals. Spearman correlations were computed between the signed average salience map and each receptor expression map.

Each correlation was permutation-corrected using a latent-space spin procedure analogous to cortical surface map rotations.88 Subject-level latent salience maps were rotated with random affine transformations prior to upsampling and spatial normalization. These upsampled maps were averaged to generate null group-level salience maps, which were correlated with each receptor expression map. Empirical p-values were defined as the proportion of null correlations exceeding the observed correlation. To account for multiple comparisons across all expression profiles, p-values were Bonferroni-corrected. Correlations with corrected p < 0.05 were reported.

Cortical Thickness based Lesion Network Mapping
To study whether model predictions align with large-scale brain network disruptions related to brain atrophy in non-responders to VNS, we employed a lesion network mapping (LNM) approach. Areas of cortical atrophy (relative to healthy age- and sex-matched subjects) were considered the “lesions”.

To evaluate potential site-related batch effects in the cortical thickness data, we applied t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding89 (t-SNE) to all cortical vertex values and estimated total intracranial volumes (eTIV), projecting them into two dimensions. To preserve local neighbourhood structure in high-dimensional data, t-SNE was selected. Although t-SNE does not preserve global distances well, it offers an established and effective visualization tool for our goal of exploring relative clustering and assessing potential batch effects. Embeddings were visualized by site (Supplementary Fig. 9a), outcome, and age (Supplementary Fig. 9b–c). Age showed the strongest correlation with t-SNE component 1 (Supplementary Fig. 9d). As no consistent clustering by site was observed, no further harmonization was applied.

Mapping regions of brain atrophy to a common network with normative structural connectivity
We sought to delineate whether spatially distributed atrophic regions in individuals map onto a common brain network associated with VNS response. To this end, we employed LNM.90 We generated parametric maps to quantify each subject’s vertex-wise cortical thickness deviations from a normative population of 2382 children (Hospital for Sick Children, n=393, ABIDE,62 n=338, HBN,62 n=1371, Calgary Preschool,63 n=251, Cam-CAN,64 n=29, age 1.9 to 25.0 years, 63% male). We fit first-order linear models for age and eTIV for each sex at each vertex in the normative dataset and applied them to the VNS cohort. Cohort residuals were then normalized to the normative residual distribution to derive age-, eTIV-, and sex-adjusted z-scores, which we termed 𝑣-scores. Each subject’s 𝑣-map (full width at half maximum (FWHM) = 3mm) was thresholded at 𝑣 ≤ −1.64 and binarized to generate the “lesion” map for LNM. Subjects were excluded if the atrophic vertex count exceeded 5% (Supplementary Fig. 10a) of the total brain surface (n = 5) to minimize the confounding effects of global atrophy. After applying this threshold and FreeSurfer segmentation quality-based exclusion criterion, 115 of 263 subjects were retained for lesion network mapping analyses. The remaining subjects were excluded either for failed FreeSurfer reconstruction or incomplete sex information.

To perform lesion network mapping (LNM), we used a subset of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) diffusion MRI dataset68 (n = 218, age < 25). Diffusion data were preprocessed using TractoFlow, 91 which performs denoising, motion and eddy current correction, B0 normalization, and fibre response function (FRF) estimation. Tractography was performed using Particle Filtering Tractography (PFT)92 with interface-based seeding (60 seeds/voxel), a minimum streamline length of 5 mm, maximum of 200 mm, and spherical harmonics order 8. Only the b=1000 s/mm² shell was used. Mean FRFs were disabled to improve multi-site harmonization.

Cortical surfaces were generated using FreeSurfer v6.0 as part of the freesurfer_flow pipeline. Surface-Enhanced Tractography93 (SET) was then applied using probabilistic fODFs from TractoFlow, with an anatomically informed stopping criterion at the grey–white junction to minimize gyral bias. Streamlines were further filtered using convex optimization modeling for microstructure informed tractography94 (COMMIT) to retain only those contributing meaningfully to the diffusion signal.

Processing was implemented via Nextflow95 workflows and Singularity96 containers, using publicly available images from the Sherbrooke Connectivity Imaging Lab (https://scil.usherbrooke.ca/).

Each VNS subject’s binarized atrophy map was used to filter HCP tractograms, retaining only streamlines intersecting the atrophic cortex. The endpoints of these streamlines were projected to MNI space (1 mm³ resolution).97 Atrophy networks were defined by combining endpoint maps across all HCP subjects and retaining voxels present in ≥20% of subjects. This thresholding approach was conceptually adapted from the disconnectome framework,98 but tailored to the endpoint-based tractography analyses used in our study. Voxel-wise t-tests were performed comparing responders and non-responders across all non-zero voxels, with statistical significance determined via 3DClustSim99 (voxel-wise p < 0.05, cluster-level α = 0.05).

Mapping regions of brain atrophy to a common network with normative functional connectivity
To assess functional connectivity patterns associated with regional atrophy, we used the same atrophy maps described above as seed regions in a normative resting-state fMRI connectome. Preprocessed fMRI data were obtained from the Brain Genomics Superstruct Project (n = 1000).100 Preprocessing was conducted by the data providers and included removal of the first 4 volumes, slice-time and motion correction (MCFLIRT), exclusion of frames with framewise displacement > 0.2 mm or DVARS > 50, co-registration to anatomical images, regression of nuisance signals (motion, global signal, CSF, and white matter), bandpass filtering (0.0009–0.08 Hz), and projection to MNI-152 2 mm space.

For each VNS subject, the average BOLD timeseries from the subject’s atrophy map was extracted and used as a seed in voxel-wise linear regression across the normative dataset using AFNI’s 3dDeconvolve.99 Correlation coefficients were Fisher-transformed to Z-scores, and voxelwise t-statistics were computed, yielding one statistical map per subject (n = 115). These maps were compared between responders and non-responders using a voxel-wise generalized linear model implemented in FSL’s randomise,101 controlling for total atrophy volume. The resulting group-level statistical map was used in subsequent analyses assessing spatial concordance with the VQ-VAE model salience map.

Assessment of Network Concordance with Salience Map
To evaluate the spatial concordance between predictive salience maps and normative brain networks, we performed a voxel-wise overlap analysis using response-associated functional and structural connectivity networks derived from resting-state fMRI and diffusion tractography, respectively. All network maps were aligned to MNI space and resampled to 1 mm isotropic resolution.

We computed the mean of the element-wise product between the salience map and the structural and functional network maps to quantify the empirical spatial concordance. To test whether the spatial concordance was statistically significant, we leveraged the aforementioned latent-space spin permutation procedure, adapted from methods for rotating cortical surface maps to maintain spatial autocorrelation76 (Supplementary Fig. 12a). Subject-level latent salience maps were randomly rotated using affine transformations (consistent affine across all subjects per permutation), upsampled to image space via trilinear interpolation, and registered to MNI space using each subject’s pre-computed nonlinear warp. The resulting rotated maps were averaged across subjects to generate null group-level salience maps (n = 1000). For each, alignment was quantified using the same structural and functional procedures applied to the observed data, yielding a null distribution of concordance values. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05 based on the proportion of null values exceeding the observed concordance, with the 95th percentile visualized for context.

### Reviewer 1

Aims:
In this manuscript, the authors seek to produce a predictive model of VNS response using T1w MRI. Specifically, this model
provides reasonable predictive power on paediatric cases binarising response between <=20 and >=80 seizure reduction,
although this effect is reduced when using more traditional outcomes (<50 and >=50 seizure reduction, respectively). They
identify areas key to their model’s prediction of response (thalamic, brainstem, insula, and peri-Rolandic) notably these
correlate well with regions known to be affected by VNS (VagAN). This work paves the way for the use of T1w MRI in
presurgical evaluation for VNS in paediatric cohorts.
This study has many positives, and I congratulate the authors for this impressive work. The study is novel in both its
methods, data, and hypotheses. The sample size is huge compared to previous work, and the growing use of VNS makes it
timely. I consider the field of VNS research in epilepsy to be extremely worthwhile, and hope my comments can help
improve the authors improve this important study.
Major Points:
1. The methodology in this paper is interesting as an application of modern machine learning tools. However, it would also
be good to know if simpler statistical analyses of basic measures are similarly informative (e.g. volume/surface
area/thickness measures from freesurfer). Looking at figure 3c, perhaps thalamic volume alone is already somewhat
informative?
2. If I understood correctly, the 39 patients in the withheld test data was chosen randomly. This withheld data of 39 patients
represents only one of the possible sets of 39 patients that could be held-out. It would give more confidence in the approach
if this could be permuted many times and error bars plotted on figure 3b, along with confidence intervals for AUCs.
3a Following on from point 2 regarding test data. I think it would be worthwhile to test generalisability across data from
different hospitals. I.e. hold out data from one hospital and train on the others, then report test accuracy on the withheld
hospital. This would be useful to know since it will tell us if the model can be used/transferred to other hospitals, which
would be clinically important.
3b. Continuing from point 3a, are there any hospitals with data to which the model/approach does not generalise to very
well? If so why? (perhaps they have older/younger demographics? Poorer scan quality?)
4. The authors focus their evaluation mainly on AUC. This is important, and I have no problem with this. I think it might also
be worthwhile reporting if the specificity at 100% sensitivity and vice versa. I think this would be worthwhile because this
may be useful for either ruling out definite non-responders, or perhaps as a screening tool for identifying/prioritising likely
responders.
5. The regions identified as having a “Higher” feature value for prediction using the gradient-based saliency mapping are not
provided with a quantitative backing. Providing a numerical underpinning to justify the chosen regions would provide greater
confidence and understanding of whether these regions are uniquely involved or if the whole brain is still required. N.b. this
could potentially be partly addressed through point 1 above.
Minor Points:
Reference 8 and reference 32 are the same (I have not checked, but it is possible this occurs more than once).
It is surprising given prior literature that you find so many individuals with >=80% and <=20% seizure reduction. Historically
these rates appeared far lower. Do you have any knowledge as to why this combined North American cohort appears to
have significantly more individuals at both extremities of response?
It is not identified how seizure reduction was calculated. Assumedly, this is through seizure diaries or discussed at follow-up
appointments which should be clarified.
Within the methods you refer to training cohorts both as training and discovery cohorts consistent naming would be clearer.
“Subjects with significant anomalies, prior neurosurgical intervention (Supplementary Fig. 3a-d), or conflicting outcome
assessments, were excluded. After filtering, the final dataset comprised 263 subjects”. The exact number dropped for each of
these reasons would be interesting. A PRISMA flow diagram would be helpful as a supplementary figure.
figure 4d; top row, middle panel, the Insula arrow terminates in the putamen at the moment.
“ Each four-dimensional latent tensor (spatial dimensions × feature channels) was spatially averaged across the x, y, and z
axes, yielding a single 32-dimensional feature vector per subject. “ I struggled to follow/understand the rationale for the
averaging across the spatial axes xyz. Please can you explain this in more detail? Perhaps in an expanded supplementary
methods.
figure 2g -I did not follow what is relative volume. relative to what? The responder blue bars on the chart are all at 100%, so I
assume it’s relative to the responder. Perhaps it would be helpful to plot relative to healthy control and show a synthetic
control in figure 2f for reference
I thought the validation in the TLE cohort was a brilliant idea. I was wondering what the interpretation would be if the model
had generalised to the TLE cohort. Do you think that would indicate shared mechanisms of response to VNS and also
response to TLE surgery? As such, should we conclude that given the model did not generalise to TLE the mechanisms
differ?

### Reviewer 2

Recommendation:
Major Revisions
Title:
A Deep Representation Learning Model to Predict Response to Vagus Nerve Stimulation
Overview and general recommendation:
This work investigated the use of T1-weighted MRI data for predicting clinical response to implantable vagus nerve
stimulation (VNS) therapy in individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy. The authors leveraged their access to a network of
clinical neuroimaging databases to aggregate a large cohort of preoperative and postoperative (resections etc.) T1w-MRI
scans, which were then used for modeling development. A vector quantized variational autoencoder was used to model the
latent space of input imaging data. Subsequently, an SVM classifier was trained on the reduced latent features to predict
treatment outcome, as binary classes: responder(>80% seizure reduction) or non-responder (<20% seizure reduction).
Modeling results indicate that with this dataflow, the SVM can predict VNS response above chance levels (AUC = 0.73).
Given the lack of robust, reliable presurgical bio/markers of response to implantable VNS, this work represents a valuable
step toward the development of preoperative, neuroimaging-informed clinical decision making in treating pediatric epilepsy
with VNS. In addition to aggregating a large cohort, the authors further attempt to localize relevant anatomical and functional
correlates of response by examining the model’s learned representations, informing further clinical explorations and
highlighting the utility of presurgical T1w MRI scans.
The manuscript is clinically valuable and generally well-written with most methods detailed. However, given the difficulty in
reproducing this work (closed data due to patient privacy), there are several critical aspects of the methodology, evaluation,
and presentation that require significant clarification and refinement to improve transparency, and reproducibility. These
factors along with some unsupported discussion claims detract from the main message of the manuscript and require
titration.
Major Concerns
Feedback
• The organizations of the manuscript and its comparisons are disjointed, and their presentation is confusing. The
manuscript would benefit from improved organization. For example, combine all modeling steps into one figure with subparts
and clearly label inputs, sizes, transformations etc. Outcomes can be ported to another figure.
• The work centers on presenting a framework for predicting VNS response called VQ-VNS, which presumably includes the
encoding/decoding model (VQ-VAE) and then the SVM. The use of “VQ” in naming the framework leaves room for confusion
as it’s suggestive of only the encoding/decoding aspect of modeling (Is this framework specific to only using an SVM post
encoding?). I suggest renaming or explaining explicitly what the framework is and isn’t for clarity.
• There are several models fit throughout the manuscript (OLS, Linear-SVM, etc.). The manuscript would benefit from a
structured comparison between a progression of models fit on clinical variables then latent features. For example, fitting a
simple logistic regression model on the clinical variables, and SVM, and SVM with anatomical information, then SVM as
well as other ensemble/ explainable models on latent space features. The AUC and other metrics for this should be
compared within one figure.
• Throughout the manuscript avoid nonspecific references like “the model,” be specific with model type or model variation as
it becomes confusing.
• The lack of cross-validation or presentation of variation throughout the manuscript is concerning. Please apply these
techniques where possible and report outcomes with quantified variation.
• Figure 1c includes subjects over the age of 20, can you explain their inclusion? The manuscript could benefit from a
deeper/more explicit discussion of the heterogenous age distribution of subjects and how this variation could affect
indications of atrophy and findings related to serotonin networks.
• Please revise the claims on lines 206-208. The model’s poor performance on out-of-distribution data generally does not
suggest any specificity to VNS, especially given that the model was pre trained on healthy non-VNS patients. This likely
reflects domain shift or lack of representativeness in training data, and less likely biological specificity.
• Throughout the manuscript please be explicit about dimensions and sizes where possible. For example, lines 194-195:
“spatial dimension” could be made clearer with subscripts x,y,z.
• Explain the choice and dimensionality of the 32-dimension feature space on line 196.
Figures
• The manuscript would greatly benefit from a figure illustrating the full model development process: from pretraining, to
feature extraction, to SVM training and prediction. Each step should also include dimensionality of data flow, especially
input, output, codebook, and latent volumes.
• Figure 1g and Figure 3b both have labels for “VNS” but demonstrate modeling results for two different models. Please use
better labels in figure legends to better distinguish between different types of models used.
• Figure 2g borders on visual exaggeration. Please plot x-axis from zero and have a zoomed-in subpanel or use a different
plot type. Please also clarify how data from this figure were acquired. For example if this is an aggregate measure across
subjects, please show variations across generations for each region.
Modeling
• Explain the choice of using an SVM as the classifier for the embeddings rather than an ensemble of models or other
alternatives (random forest etc.). I strongly suggest comparing different modeling strategies, where applicable.
• Please include a full suite of model assessment metrics where applicable (Accuracy, F1, Precision, Recall, etc.)
• For each subset of data (test, validation, test) please explicitly provide the distribution of responders and non-responders
and be explicit about data imbalances and highlight mitigation strategies.
• Add reconstruction scores to the images shown
• In supplemental figure 3, please double check that the cases shown in a-d do in fact correspond to the inputs in panel e
• Ensure all mathematical equations are fully defined and explained with all parameters clearly labeled.
• In the UMAP embeddings the manifold shows some separation of data. Were those data points inspected further to
determine which factors could have contributed to their separation? If so, please explain or suggest possible separation
factors.
• Methodological details tend to be lacking or missing for secondary comparisons. For example, in examining subjects with
between 20%-80% seizure reduction, evaluating reconstruction with abnormal imaging etc. Please provide additional details
and organize carefully.
• For lines 527-530, please reword for improved clarity.
• Please clarify/detail assessment steps used for subjects between 20%-80% seizure reduction.
• In evaluating the cortical thickness estimation, explain the choice behind using t-SNE vs other techniques. What are its
benefits and shortcomings?
• Explain the choice between permuting model outcomes versus other model comparison techniques.
• In order to improve potential clinical applicability, consider framing predictions as probability scores of response (e.g.
P(Response|Input)) rather than binary outputs.
Data and Code
• I strongly suggest porting the model weights over to a more stable, permanent repository rather than its current form, which
is inaccessible. Some domain appropriate archives include OpenNeuro, Zenodo, etc.
• This work would greatly benefit from a demonstrative Jupyter notebook. This could potentially be shown with anonymized
or synthetically generated responder/non-responder T1w MRI scans, which are then used to demonstrate feature extraction,
visualization, and then prediction with the trained classifiers.
Minor Concerns
Figures
• Please unionize all the font types across figures and sub panels
• Double check that figures conform to the journal's guidelines (i.e. font sizes etc.)
• For figure 1d, discretize colors, space them out more and add the rounded percentages to the corresponding block for
clarity. For example, if “Development Delay” accounts for 90% of subjects please label the bar with the corresponding
percentage. Under each label add the type of outcome (i.e. binary, continuous, etc.)
• Figure 1d please make axes square for clearer visual comparison
• Figure 1c, please add the sample size for each subgroup (responders/non-responders). Can be added inside the plot
under each group or centered under the corresponding label.
Results
• Add min and max age ranges where applicable

### Reviewer 3

Clinical
Researchers developed VQ-VNS, a deep learning model that predicts the effectiveness of vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) for
children with epilepsy using routine preoperative MRI scans. Traditional clinical data could not predict treatment response,
but VQ-VNS achieved significant predictive accuracy and highlighted serotonin-rich brain regions and connectivity
disruptions in non-responders. These results are clinically relevant and highly translational, offering a biologically
interpretable tool to guide decisions and reduce unnecessary invasive procedures.
Methods
Patient grouping: Participants were divided into >80% seizure reduction vs. <20%. What about patients between these cut-
offs? Excluding ~350 patients (694/1046 included) seems a large data loss. Since you collected seizure frequency reduction
as a continuous variable, would correlating with this continuous measure be more informative?
Clinical outcomes: In the analysis section, you note that including patients with ambiguous outcomes did not improve SVM
performance. This is an important observation — why not include them in the main analysis if results are unchanged?
Please clarify the added value of excluding them.
Clinical variables: Have magnet effects and quality of life (QOL) been addressed? Both are well-established as clinically
relevant (Danthine V., Boon P.), and could enrich the dataset. If available, these should be included.
SVM classifier: Only 263 patients were included after excluding those with prior surgery or significant abnormalities. Please
describe their clinical characteristics. Were they representative of the larger cohort (e.g., intellectual disability, DEEs,
epilepsy duration)? The generalizability of the model is limited if large patient groups are excluded.
TLE cohort: It is unclear why specificity analyses were limited to a TLE subgroup. Were these patients outside the
CONNECTIVOS trial? Were they seizure free? Why not include other surgical subgroups (e.g., ETLE)?
Methodological consistency: For the VNS analysis, patients with brain lesions were excluded. Is this a methodological
requirement, and if so, why would it not apply to the surgical cohort? Would comparison to a DBS cohort (ANT, CM) be more
appropriate than only TLE?
Definitions: How was developmental delay defined, and does this overlap with DEE cases?
Parameters: The discussion states VNS was “optimally programmed.” Please define this — were parameters such as rapid
cycling or saturation cycling considered (e.g., Norpulse study)?
Data splitting: The dataset was split 80/10/10 for training/validation/test. What is the rationale for this choice? Did results vary
with different splits (e.g., 50/25/25)? Please provide references or justification.
PET-derived neurotransmitter maps: The description of PET-based receptor/transporter profiles across nine systems is
intriguing. Were these data specifically acquired for this study, or part of a pre-existing dataset? This is not fully described in
the “pretraining data compilation” section.
Results / Discussion
The finding of serotonergic large-scale network disruptions is novel and important. However, the lack of results for the locus
coeruleus–noradrenergic system is surprising, given its strong support in both human (P300, pupillometry) and animal
studies (Raedt, Krahl). Could the authors comment on this apparent discrepancy?
The statement that “beyond optimal programming, there are no associations between increased charge density and
outcome” (ref 59) may need qualification. Recent work, including Fahoum et al. (Brain Stimulation, 2022), suggests
optimal intensity correlates with outcomes, especially in pediatric cohorts. Please reconcile with this evidence.
Details
The section on region-based morphometry would be clearer if you specify whether this refers to VBM, SBM, or other
approaches.
The statement “region-based morphometry is constrained by atlas-based parcellations…” requires a proper reference. If
reference 15 already supports this, please move it to the end of the sentence; if not, an additional reference is needed.
Conclusion:
In its current form, the manuscript is technically strong and demonstrates the use of highly specialized methodologies.
However, the presentation may be difficult for clinicians and readers outside the computational field to fully grasp. If the
authors aim for a high-impact journal and a broad audience, we encourage them to simplify and clarify the description of the
methods, and to place greater emphasis on the biological and clinical interpretation of their findings — particularly the role of
the implicated networks and neurotransmitter systems. This would considerably enhance the accessibility, readability, and
overall impact of the work.
Summary Methodological/Engeneering
The manuscript introduces the VQ-VNS framework, a methodology designed to predict and classify responses to vagus
nerve stimulation (VNS) in pediatric populations. The framework builds on the VQ-VAE architecture and incorporates
interpretability mechanisms by adapting SHAP and Grad-CAM. Identifying likely responders has the potential to minimize
the need for invasive procedures.
A key limitation of the study is that the proposed methodology is presented with substantial technical complexity, but with
limited benchmarking against alternative approaches.
Major Comments
- The authors reference several alternative approaches for responder identification [11–15]. A comparative table would help
quantify the accuracy improvements of the proposed framework, particularly in relation to other T1-weighted MRI–based
predictive models.
- The manuscript states: “The resulting archetypal non-responder showed reduced grey matter, white matter, and subcortical
volumes, together with ventricular enlargement.” If such morphological alterations are discriminative, why would automated
segmentation of T1-weighted images not provide an equally effective classification of responders? A comparison with
standard volumetric and morphometric approaches would strengthen the contribution of the proposed framework.
- The original spin permutation procedure rotated cortical surface maps while preserving contralateral symmetry. Was this
constraint maintained in the present experiments? Furthermore, the original test statistic excluded non-cortical regions. Were
such regions incorporated in the current analysis? These methodological details require clarification.
Minor Comments
- The statement that prognostic signatures are “likely embedded in subtle, distributed, and nonlinear anatomical patterns”
would benefit from supporting references.
- The rationale for selecting an SVM classifier should be expanded, in comparison with other machine learning methods
(e.g., random forests, k-nearest neighbors).
- The contribution of individual components within the composite loss function could be clearer. Ablation experiments
comparing performance with and without each term could justify their inclusion.
- The claim that “the model’s reconstructions preserved fine anatomical details” appears somewhat contradictory, since VQ-
VAE models are known to lose fine-scale structural information. A more precise description of which features are preserved
or lost would enhance interpretability.
- The observation that “reconstruction fidelity was lower in subjects with significant structural abnormalities” raises the
question of whether this reduction affects classification performance. Are response predictions less reliable for patients with
pronounced abnormalities?
- Additionally, the reconstruction fidelity of the CONNECTiVOS pediatric epilepsy cohort should be reported.
- Gradient-based saliency mapping seems to implicate more regions than those emphasized in the text (thalami, brainstem,
insular cortex, peri-Rolandic regions). How were the reported regions identified and selected (e.g., thresholding criteria, local
maxima)?
- Differences between synthetic responders and non-responders in Figure 2F are visually subtle. Enhancing or highlighting
these differences would improve interpretability.
- “The model’s attention was concentrated within brain regions enriched in serotonin transporter (5-HTT) expression”. Can
you quantify this result?
- “To assess the predictive value of clinical data, a support vector machine (SVM) was trained on 80% of the dataset
(discovery cohort, n = 550) to predict VNS outcome, with the remaining 20% held out for validation (n = 144)”. Was there an
independent test set? Clarification is needed.
- “Structure-wise agreement was evaluated across four tissue classes – grey matter, white matter, subcortical grey matter,
and ventricles – by computing the Pearson correlation between reconstructed and original volumes across subjects”. This
only accounts for the volume size of each tissue type and not their location. Adding the DICE scores or an equivalent would
provide a more comprehensive assessment.
- “Atrophy networks were defined by combining endpoint maps across all HCP subjects”. Why were endpoints chosen
instead of complete streamlines?
- A visualization of the cortical atrophy map should be included for completeness.

### Reviewer 4

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

reviewer_updating.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Implantable neurotechnologies are increasingly used to reduce seizure burden in epilepsy. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), the most common option, is effective for only half of patients, with no means to predict outcome prior to surgery. As a result, many children undergo invasive and costly procedures without benefit. Although T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (T1w) is routinely acquired presurgically and may capture structural brain differences relevant to treatment outcome, its high dimensionality relative to sample sizes has limited its utility in predictive modeling. To address this challenge, we present VQ-VNS, a deep representation learning model to predict VNS outcome based on preoperative T1w (n=263). First, we present data from the largest pediatric VNS cohort (n=1046), wherein presurgical clinical data could not predict response (AUC 0.54,p>0.99). Next, VQ-VNS was pretrained on 7433 T1w images to learn compact anatomical representations enabling its classifier to predict VNS response (AUC=0.73,p=0.007). Model predictions localized to serotonin-rich brain regions and inferred large-scale disruptions in network connectivity among non-responders. This biologically-interpretable predictor based on routine structural imaging improves upon current clinical decision-making.

---

## Introduction

Epilepsy is the most common serious neurological disorder in children.1 The medical and psychosocial burden of drug-resistant epilepsy2 (DRE) has driven the increased usage of implantable neurotechnologies to improve seizure control. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is the most commonly recommended device,3 supported by decades of clinical experience in pediatric populations. VNS has been shown to reduce seizure frequency,4 improve quality of life,5 and decrease mortality.2 However, only half of patients realize a benefit after treatment, and clinicians are currently unable to identify responders to VNS prior to surgery,6–8 leading to unnecessary, invasive, and costly procedures. Given that there is little variability in implantation technique,9 heterogenous outcomes are likely related to intrinsic differences among patients – particularly in brain structure and function. There is an unmet need to presurgically identify responders to VNS to personalize treatment options.

T1-weighted (T1w) MRI, a routine component of presurgical evaluation in pediatric epilepsy,10 represents a high-dimensional feature space ( R > 6 million voxels per image) that may contain complex, prognostically-relevant biomarkers. However, it remains underutilized in predictive modelling, as prognostic signatures are likely embedded in subtle, distributed, and nonlinear anatomical patterns11–13 – challenges compounded by the modest sample sizes typical of pediatric imaging datasets. Approaches to identify VNS responders based on coarse imaging features such as the presence of lesions14,15 or structural etiologies of epilepsy15–17 have not been informative and reported inconsistent associations. Region-based morphometry,18 is constrained by atlas-based parcellations that fail to capture diffuse, whole-brain patterns and yields weak associations with outcome. Crucially, there are no studies that have developed predictive models for VNS response on an individual patient level that are suitable for clinical use.8 Consequently, structural imaging has yet to be adopted as a viable predictor of VNS response.

Recent advances in generative modelling have enabled self-supervised learning of compact whole-brain embeddings from high-dimensional imaging data, capturing subtle and distributed anatomical patterns without reliance on predefined features. Architectures such as vector-quantized variational autoencoders19 (VQ-VAEs) and latent diffusion models20 have leveraged these lower dimensional representations to synthesize realistic brain images while modelling interindividual variability.21,22 While primarily developed for image synthesis, these models' principal utility in clinical contexts lies in their ability to learn compressed, semantically rich representations of whole-brain anatomy. Yet, their application to clinical prediction tasks remains underexplored.23 Moreover, most prior work has focused on adult datasets – such as the UK BioBank24 – with limited attention to pediatric populations despite their increased neurodevelopmental variability.25

In addition to technical barriers, clinical deployment of deep learning in neuroimaging is often limited by clinician apprehension about model opacity. Interpretability is increasingly viewed as a prerequisite for clinical adoption.26 Consequently, there is growing interest in addressing this requirement by either developing inherently interpretable models or applying post hoc analyses to explain the outputs of models not explicitly designed for interpretability.27 In the context of implantable neurotechnologies, where treatment decisions often involve surgical risk and uncertainty, predictive models must offer both accuracy and mechanistic transparency, grounded in neurobiological plausibility.

In this work, we present VQ-VNS, a clinically focused deep learning framework for predicting response to VNS directly from presurgical T1w MRI. Our approach combines a VQ-VAE, trained to learn discrete whole-brain anatomical representations, followed by a linear support vector machine28 (SVM) classifier for outcome prediction. To provide interpretability, we integrate gradient-weighted class activation mapping29 (Grad-CAM) and Shapley additive explanations30 (SHAP) to generate voxel-level predictive salience maps. To examine the neurobiological mechanisms underlying model performance, we also related the salience maps to normative neurochemical brain architectures as well as large-scale brain networks disrupted in non-responders using normative connectomic data. Our results demonstrate that interpretable deep representation learning can be leveraged to predict VNS outcomes while offering insight into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying treatment response.

## Results

Clinical data do not predict response after VNS
We compiled the largest database of children to undergo VNS (n = 1046) from 11 North American centers through the Connectomics and Vagus Nerve Stimulation Outcome Study (CONNECTiVOS, Fig. 1a).28 Participants were deemed responders if seizure frequency was reduced by ≥80% and non-responders if ≤20% (n = 694, Fig. 1b) to reflect the bimodal distribution of seizure outcomes and mitigate the effects of ambiguous intermediate outcomes.29 The mean [SD; range] age was 10.6 [4.7; 0.8-24.2] years, 54% male and included 51% responders (Fig. 1b-c). This age range was included to capture the full developmental trajectory of brain maturation amongst pediatric and young adult populations that undergo VNS.

We first examined the association of each presurgical clinical variable with response by applying ordinary least squares regression (Fig. 1d; Supplementary Fig. 1). No clinical features were significantly associated with VNS outcome after false discovery rate correction (Supplementary Table 1). Nonlinear embedding of the clinical data using uniform manifold approximation and projection31 (UMAP) also failed to separate responders and non-responders (Fig. 1e; s = –2.7 × 10-4, p = 0.71), which was also corroborated by principal component analysis which revealed low explained variance (<12% for PC1) and no systematic response associated differences (Supplementary Fig. 2, Supplementary Table 2). Labelling the UMAP embeddings by treatment site revealed visually apparent but objectively weak (s = –0.04, p > 0.99) site-specific groupings (Fig. 1f), indicative of subtle inter-site variability in patient selection criteria without strong site-level effects.

Finally, consistent with findings in smaller cohorts,6,8 an SVM model trained on presurgical clinical features – including demographics, epilepsy history, and electroencephalography – was unable to distinguish responders to VNS from non-responders beyond chance-level performance (AUC = 0.54, p > 0.99; Fig. 1g). Furthermore, there was no difference in output current (1.9  0.7 vs. 1.7  0.7; t(101) = -1.4; p = 0.17; n = 103) or duty cycle (21  10% vs. 19  10%; t(101) = -1.3, p = 0.2, n = 103) between responders and non-responders.

Self-supervised representation learning captures anatomical patterns associated with VNS outcome
To study whether structural brain differences could predict outcome, we developed VQ-VNS, a deep representation learning model to identify VNS responders based on standard T1w sequences (Fig. 2). Because each T1w MRI scan contains over six million voxels – far exceeding the sample sizes of most pediatric epilepsy datasets (typically < 100 patients per center)32 – dimensionality reduction is critical to mitigate overfitting and enable effective model training. However, conventional approaches to dimensionality reduction, such as region-based parcellation, are insufficient to model the relationship between structural alterations and response following VNS (Supplementary Tables 3-4). Thus, the VQ-VNS model consists of two stages: 1) a VQ-VAE19 architecture compresses the high-dimensional MRI data into a compact latent representation, and (2) a support vector machine (SVM) classifies patients based on these latent features. The VQ-VAE architecture is well suited to compressing complex anatomical data into compact latent representations.21 We trained this model on large datasets of healthy subjects and persons with epilepsy who had not received VNS (n = 7,433; Fig. 2a–c). These datasets included participants across the lifespan (age 1.9 - 88.9 years) and contained a wide range of anatomical and acquisition-related variability to support the VQ-VAE’s ability to learn robust, generalizable representations. We optimized the VQ-VAE model with a composite loss term – comprising mean absolute error, perceptual loss,33 spectral loss34, commitment loss19 and an adversarial term derived from a discriminator35 model – to generate high-quality reconstructions of the input T1w image. This composite loss function was based on prior experiments21 where extensive ablations were performed to evaluate the contribution of each loss component.

The VQ-VAE’s reconstructions preserved anatomical details and captured biologically meaningful variation (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Fig. 3). We evaluated reconstruction fidelity using established metrics, including multiscale structural similarity36 (MS-SSIM), Fréchet Inception Distance37 (FID), and mean squared error (MSE). The VQ-VAE demonstrated strong performance (Supplementary Table 5), with a mean (SD) MS-SSIM of 0.97 (0.01), FID of 1.5 × 10-3 (1.2 × 10-3), and an MSE of 3.7 × 10-3 (8.6 × 10-4). To assess anatomical plausibility, we segmented both original and reconstructed images using SynthSeg38 and computed structure-wise correlations and Dice-Sørensen coefficients across four tissue classes: grey matter, white matter, subcortical grey matter, and ventricles. The VQ-VAE reconstructions demonstrated high correlation with true volumes across all four classes, with Pearson correlation coefficients ranging from 0.96 to 1.00 (Fig. 3b); furthermore, the reconstructions exhibited strong spatial overlap, yielding mean Dice-Sørensen coefficients ranging from 0.78 to 0.91 (Supplementary Table 6). Reconstruction fidelity was lower in subjects with significant structural abnormalities (Fig. 3a; Supplementary Fig. 4) with a mean (SD) SSIM of 0.95 (0.01), FID of 4.1 × 10-3 (9.8 × 10-4), and MSE of 4.7 × 10-3 (9.2 × 10-3), consistent with the VQ-VAE being trained primarily on anatomically typical brains.

Finally, we assessed whether this learned latent space captured features associated with VNS response without additional training. We encoded each subject’s image from the training subset of children who underwent VNS in the CONNECTiVOS cohort (199 of 263 images, Supplementary Fig. 5), computed the median latent representations separately for responders and non-responders, quantized these representations, and decoded them to generate synthetic archetypal brains (Fig. 3c). Compared to the archetypal responder, the resulting archetypal non-responder showed reduced grey matter, white matter and subcortical volumes, together with ventricular enlargement (Fig. 3d). These differences suggest that the latent representations captured structural features relevant to treatment outcome without direct optimization for VNS outcome prediction and that VNS non-responders exhibit lower brain volumes (i.e. atrophy) compared to responders.

Latent representations support accurate prediction and spatial interpretation of VNS outcome
To evaluate the predictive utility of the latent space for response following VNS, we trained a linear SVM classifier (Fig. 2e) using quantized latent vectors from the frozen VQ-VAE encoder. To reduce dimensionality, each four-dimensional latent tensor (x, y, and z spatial dimensions × feature channels) was spatially averaged across the x, y, and z axes, yielding a single 32-dimensional21 feature vector per subject. Each element of this vector therefore captures the global magnitude of the respective latent feature learned from the underlying T1w image. We then applied two-sided t-test-based feature selection on the training data (n = 199) to retain 27 of the 32 latent features (Supplementary Table 7), which were used to train the SVM, which demonstrated the strongest predictive performance among multiple classifiers (Supplementary Fig. 6). To assess the stability and significance of the learned features, we first trained 1000 SVM classifiers on randomly partitioned subsets of the VNS cohort. The mean AUC across models was significantly greater than that expected under the null distribution (mean AUC = 0.61; t(1998) = 28.6, p = 1e-150; Fig. 3e), suggesting that the latent representations carried measurable predictive signal.

We then trained a final SVM classifier using the training (n = 199) and validation (n = 25) subsets of the VNS cohort and tested on an independent held-out set (n = 39). The resulting model achieved an AUC of 0.73 in predicting response to VNS (permutation p = 0.007; Fig. 3f; Supplementary Fig. 7; Supplementary Table 8). The model maintained its predictive capacity across diverse age groups and treatment centers (Supplementary Fig. 7C). Model performance remained robust with the inclusion of subjects with ambiguous outcomes binarized at the 50% seizure reduction threshold (n = 53; AUC = 0.67, permutation p = 0.02; Supplementary Fig. 8). To evaluate the classifier’s ability to generalize across acquisition sites, we performed site hold-out validation, in which all images from one site were excluded during training and used exclusively for testing (Supplementary Table 9). Sites contributing small sample sizes were combined to create a single evaluation set. The classifiers achieved above chance accuracy (0.61 to 0.67), suggesting site-invariant structural features predictive of VNS response.

To evaluate the specificity of the SVM to predicting VNS outcomes, we tested its performance on an independent cohort of children who underwent temporal lobectomy for temporal lobe epilepsy39 (n = 102; mean age [SD] = 12.8 [3.9] years; 69.6% seizure freedom). The SVM model did not predict outcomes above chance level after temporal lobectomy (AUC = 0.57, permutation p = 0.12; Fig. 3f), suggesting that its decision boundary did not generalize to this population.

To visualize brain regions contributing most to model predictions, we implemented a hybrid salience attribution method integrating SHAP30 values from the SVM with Grad-CAM29 from the VQ-VAE encoder. Subject-specific SHAP values corresponding to the 27 selected latent features were expanded to a full 32-dimensional vector by assigning zeros to the unselected features. We computed the dot product between this SHAP vector and each subject’s latent representation, and backpropagated the resulting scalar through the VQ-VAE encoder. Gradients and activations were then extracted from the final convolutional layer to produce voxel-wise salience maps. This approach enabled SVM-derived feature importance to guide spatial salience attribution in the original image space. We identified several regions of high predictive value including the thalami, brainstem, and peri-Rolandic regions (Fig. 4a).

Model salience localizes to serotonergic networks disrupted in VNS non-responders
To better understand how model predictions relate to the chemoarchitecture of the brain, we correlated the VQ-VAE model’s salience map to the topology of brain receptor and transporter densities across nine different neurotransmitter systems from over 1200 healthy individuals.40 Neurotransmitter receptors are heterogeneously distributed across the neocortex and may be modulated by implanted technologies to modify neural states and reshape network-level communication.41 Each correlation was assessed against a null distribution generated via spin permutation testing, in which a single rotational affine was applied across all subjects’ latent salience maps for each permutation, prior to upscaling and averaging (Fig. 4b). We generated 1,000 such null maps per comparison to compute empirical p-values and account for spatial autocorrelation. The VQ-VAE’s attention was concentrated within brain regions enriched in serotonin transporter (5-HTT) expression (r = 0.26, p = 0.04; Fig. 4c).

The anatomically distributed pattern of salient regions also suggested involvement of broader brain networks in VNS response. To further interpret model predictions, we leveraged lesion network mapping, an approach which links focal structural abnormalities to disruptions in large-scale brain circuitry using normative connectomic data.42 This allowed us to test whether brain atrophy in non-responders, relative to 2,382 typically developing children (age 1.9 to 25.0 years, 63% male), converged upon a common network aligned with the VQ-VNS model’s saliency profile. We first demonstrated that cortical thickness measurements did not contain site-specific batch effects (Supplementary Fig. 9) and that group-level spatial patterns of atrophy alone did not clearly distinguish responders from non-responders (Supplementary Fig. 10). Regional brain atrophy maps converged upon large-scale structural (Fig. 4d, Supplementary Fig. 11) and functional (Fig. 4e) networks that were preferentially disrupted in non-responders to VNS. The VQ-VNS model’s saliency map showed significant spatial concordance (Supplementary Fig. 12a) with these structural (p<0.001, Supplementary Fig. 12b) and functional (p=0.04, Supplementary Fig. 12c) networks following spin permutation tests. Network findings were also concordant with brain regions to which vagus afferent fibres are known to project through the nucleus tractus solitarius,32 including areas that are activated by VNS.43

## Methods

VNS Data Collection
Data were collected through a multi-institutional registry as part of the CONNECTiVOS study (Connectomic profiling and Vagus nerve stimulation Outcomes Study).59 This study involved children with epilepsy and was conducted across multiple North American sites, with local investigators engaged in design, data collection, and authorship. This study was approved by the institutional review boards of all participating sites (REB Approval Number 1000060282PID) and carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.60 Data were collected from 1046 patients who underwent VNS implantation at centers in Canada and the United States. Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are described in the CONNECTiVOS protocol. All data were collected under local ethics approval with informed consent and assent where appropriate, and were de-identified prior to analysis. No material transfer, resource-poor settings, or elevated researcher risk were involved. We did not prespecify indications for VNS implantation, and all programming parameters were at the discretion of treating physicians.

For each participant, we collected continuous data on age at VNS implantation, duration of epilepsy, and percent seizure reduction at last follow-up based on parent-reported seizure frequency. Binary variables included: sex, presence of a genetic diagnosis, developmental delay, family history of epilepsy, history of infantile spasms, congenital or acquired epilepsy etiology, and prior epilepsy surgery. EEG data included variables indicating focal versus generalized seizure onset and lateralization of interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs). Preoperative imaging data including High-resolution 3D T1-weighted (T1w) were collected both prospectively and retrospectively.

T1w MRI for the VNS cohort were acquired at either 1.5T or 3T. Scanner manufacturers include Philips, Siemens, General Electric, and Toshiba. Scanner models included Achieva, Skyra, Trio TIM, Ingenuity, Signa HDxt, Discovery MR750, Ingenia, Intera, Symphony, Prisma, Avanto, Signa Excite, Symphony TIM, Trio, Titan, Discovery MR750w, and Genesis Signa. Key parameters for T1-weighted imaging were: flip angle, 12.3° (8.0° – 40.0°); echo time, 3.7 ms (1.7 – 9.2 ms); repetition time, 7.9 ms (1.1 – 25.0 ms); and mean voxel size, 0.7x0.7x0.7mm.

Pretraining Data Compilation
We compiled data from a cohort of healthy subjects and persons with epilepsy from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE, n = 412),61 the Healthy Brain Network (HBN, n = 2081),62 the Calgary Preschool MRI (n = 265),63 the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN, n = 649),64 and the Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC, n = 923),65 SickKids internal normative dataset (n = 1260), The Imaging Database for Epilepsy And Surgery (IDEAS, n = 542),66 Focal Cortical Dysplasia Type II (FCD-2, n = 170),67 Temporal Lobe Epilepsy – UNAM (UNAM-TLE, n = 66), Human Connectome Project Young Adult (HCP, n = 1065)68 datasets for a combined dataset of 7433 images. To balance retaining a sufficient training set size with sufficient subjects for validation and robust assessment on a held-out test cohort, these data were split into training, validation and test sets in ratios of 75%, 10%, and 15% respectively, which is commonly used in the context of clinical datasets

The SickKids internal normative T1w images were acquired at either 1.5T or 3T across various scanners (Signa HDxt, GE Healthcare; Achieva, Philips Healthcare; Magnetom Skyra, Siemens Healthineers) with a dedicated head-coil. Images were acquired either in the sagittal or the axial plane: TR/TE, 6-9/2-5 ms; flip angle: 10-15 degrees, mean voxel size, 1.0x1.0x1.5 mm.

All T1w images were brain extracted,38,69 70resampled to 1mm3 isotropic resolution,71, bias field corrected, intensity normalized with Fuzzy C-means,72 and rigidly registered73 to a 1mm MNI brain extracted template (Fig. 2a).74

Analysis of clinical data
Participants were classified as non-responders if they had ≤20% seizure frequency reduction, and as responders for ≥80% seizure frequency reduction based on the bimodal distribution of treatment outcomes (Fig. 1b) and to mitigate misclassification risk inherent to seizure reporting from participants with ambiguous outcomes.75 Based on the outcome threshold, 694 of the 1046 subjects were included. We used ordinary least squares regression to model the univariable relationship between each clinical variable and VNS response. Counts of missing values for each clinical variable are presented in Supplementary Table 10. False discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied to adjust for multiple comparisons.

To model multivariable and non-linear relationships, we applied Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP).31 Silhouette scores76 quantified the clustering quality of UMAP embeddings by outcome and site, with significance assessed via one-sided one-sample t-tests. To further assess whether the observed manifold structure reflected biologically or methodologically meaningful variance, we additionally performed principal component analysis (PCA) on the same dataset. Loadings of the top principal components were examined to identify the metrics contributing most to overall variance within the clinical data. Scores for the leading components were then compared between responders and non-responders to evaluate whether these reduced dimensions captured differences associated with VNS outcome.

To assess the predictive value of clinical data, a support vector machine (SVM)36 was trained on 80% of the dataset (n = 550) to predict VNS outcome. The remaining 20% (n = 144) was held out as an independent test set to evaluate model performance after training. To ensure that both training and test sets contained only clearly defined responders and non-responders, subjects with ambiguous (intermediate) outcomes were excluded prior to this split. Recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV)77 was employed for feature selection. The clinical SVM model’s performance was quantified using area under the curve (AUC) and confusion matrices. We additionally evaluated model performance with the inclusion of subjects with ambiguous outcomes (n = 352) and observed no improvement.

Cortical Thickness Estimation and Regional-based Modelling of Response
Cortical thickness was estimated from T1-weighted images using FreeSurfer71 to derive individualized thickness maps used in all downstream atrophy and network-based analyses. Cortical surface reconstruction in FreeSurfer v7.4.2 began with an affine transformation aligning images to the MNI305 atlas, followed by B1 bias field estimation from white matter intensity variations and subsequent intensity inhomogeneity correction. Intensity normalization was then performed to correct for cross-site and cross-scanner fluctuations that would otherwise disrupt subsequent intensity-based segmentation steps. The skull was stripped, and white matter boundaries were automatically identified based on intensity and neighbour constraints. The white matter surface then underwent smoothing through tessellation and was expanded outwards to identify the boundaries of the pial surface. Cortical thickness was calculated as the average distance from a point on the smoothed white matter surface to its corresponding point on the pial surface and vice versa. The surfaces and parametric maps were spherically inflated and registered to a standard spherical atlas.78 This was followed by region-wise regression to VNS outcome with a generalized linear model accounting for age and estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV). The parcellations were derived from the Desikan-Killiany Atlas. Although this pipeline was established in adults, it has been validated for use in children,79 and all surface reconstructions were visually examined for accuracy.

Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoder
T1-weighted MRI scans are inherently high-dimensional, making it challenging to train predictive models directly on raw voxel intensities – particularly in the context of relatively small clinical imaging datasets. This necessitates an approach to represent these data in a low dimensional space without loss of detail necessary for downstream classification tasks. We implemented a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE)19 from the MONAI library to generate these lower dimensional latent representations. Compared to classical convolutional classifiers that require pretraining on surrogate labels such as age or diagnosis, using an autoencoder allowed the model to learn representations based solely on structural anatomy, without bias toward any specific pretraining objective.
